So you deserved affliction because of what you corrupted and the calamities you introduced, the greatest of which was the killing of Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both, and the intention to kill Isa, peace be upon him. ﴿To distress your faces﴾; that is, We sent against you servants of Ours to distress [your faces], by making the traces of distress visible upon them. He omitted the object of the lam because the first [clause] indicates it. ﴿And to enter the Masjid﴾; that is, al-Aqsa, to which We had brought you from Egypt over those long periods, and We gave you its lands gradually, and We made it a place of your security and might. Then We made it a place for honouring the noblest of Our creation by the Night Journey to it, and by gathering the spirits of all the prophets there, and his leading them in prayer there. And this is an allusion of threat to Quraysh, that if they do not return, He will replace their security in the Sanctuary with fear and their might with humiliation, and will bring upon them armies they have no power against. He did that in the year of the Conquest. But it was an act of honouring, not of humiliation, by the blessing of this noble Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and may he be ennobled, honoured, exalted and magnified always and forever. ﴿As they entered it﴾ (p-342) that is, the enemies, ﴿the first time﴾, with the sword, and subdued all your armies at once; ﴿and to destroy utterly﴾; that is, to ruin and devastate, with cutting up and scattering; ﴿what they conquered﴾; that is, of that [land]. It was said: "ma" is a verbal particle (masdariyya), meaning "the duration of their domination". Then "yutabbiru" would be intransitive, so its meaning is magnified. He emphasised the verb, confirmed the promise, and so said: ﴿with complete destruction﴾.

And in the Torah, [the passage] that he mentioned, indicating this last occasion, and Allah knows best, after what had passed of the indication to the first occasion alike, is: "If you do not keep and act upon all the commandments and statutes which I have written in this book, so that you fear the LORD your God and revere His glorious and awesome name, the LORD will bring upon you extraordinary plagues, and plague you and your descendants after you; and He will bring upon you all the diseases of Egypt which you feared, and they will cling to you; and every sickness and every plague that is not written in this book, the LORD will bring upon you until you are destroyed, and there will remain of your seed a small number, after their multitude which was like the stars of heaven, because you did not hearken to the voice of the LORD your God; so it will be that just as the LORD rejoiced over you and made you prosper and multiplied you, so the LORD will rejoice over you to destroy and bring you to nothing; and you will be plucked from the land which you are entering to possess it; and the LORD will scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth to the other; and there you will serve other gods, which neither you nor your fathers have known, wood and stone. Among those nations you shall find no rest, and there shall be no resting place for the sole of your foot; but the LORD will give you a trembling heart, failing of eyes, and anguish of soul; and your life shall hang in doubt before you; you shall fear day and night, and have no assurance of your life. In the morning you shall say, 'Would that it were evening!' and at evening you shall say, 'Would that it were morning!' because of the fear of your heart which you shall fear, and the sight of your eyes which you shall see. And the LORD will bring you back to Egypt in ships, by the way of which I said to you, 'You shall never see it again.' And there you shall be sold to your enemies as male and female slaves, and no one will buy you." These are the words of the covenant which the LORD commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which He made with them at Horeb. End quote.

I said that this is an indication of the second occasion, because it is a repetition of what I had mentioned for the first occasion. So taking it to indicate something other than what the first [passage] indicated is preferable, rather it may even be necessary. Then some learned Jews informed me that their scholars said likewise. And the destruction on this occasion was at the hand of Titus (p-344), after his father Vespasian had become king over the Romans and returned from the Holy Land, after the death of their king Tiberius, who had sent him to fight the Jews when they rebelled against his authority. With him was Yusuf ibn Kiryun (Josephus), one of the Jewish notables, who was among those the Jews had appointed to fight Vespasian and his men. They captured him and treated him well, so he remained among them. When Tiberius died and his companions made him king, he returned to Rome and sent his son to finish off Jerusalem, and sent Yusuf with him. This happened after the House had remained inhabited for four hundred and twenty years since the building of Ezra, peace be upon him. It did not enter the hands of the Jews after this destruction. This was three hundred and eighty years into the reign of Alexander. Their historian, in explaining this destruction, said: Titus was at Caesarea, then he went from there until he reached Yalu, and took six hundred men from the choicest of his army, and went to Jerusalem to observe the condition of the city, to view the fortress, to learn what he needed to know, and to plan affairs accordingly. He was also intent on writing to the people of Jerusalem with good words, calling them to peace, and offering them safe conduct. When he drew near the city (p-345) he found the gates closed, and no one came out of the city or entered it, because of the continuous wars among the rebels. So he found no one to address him from the people, and he turned back to his army.

He said: Some of the rebels, when they learned of Titus's coming, had gone out of the city and lay in ambush for him on part of the road. When he passed by them on his return, they surrounded him and separated him from his companions. He fought them fiercely until he escaped, after having come close to destruction. He then understood the courage and the evil that these people possessed, so he prepared his equipment for what Allah willed of the ruin of Jerusalem. Allah, Exalted is He and whose dominion is high and whose authority is mighty, had displayed to the Children of Israel matters which indicated to them the end of their affairs, had they been discerning. Among them was the appearance of a great star, with a strong light and an intense brilliance, by which Jerusalem illuminated the whole city all night long, nearly like daylight. It remained so for seven days, the duration of the Feast of Passover. The ignorant rejoiced at it, and the scholars were distressed. Among them also: at this feast they brought a cow to sacrifice, and it gave birth to a lamb, and the people were astonished at this. Among them also: the eastern gate of Jerusalem was great and heavy, and only a group could move it; but in those days they found it open every day without anyone opening it. The men accustomed to it would gather and close it, then return and find it open again. So the ignorant rejoiced and the scholars were distressed (p-346). Among them also: there appeared in the air over the House of the Holy of Holies the image of a human face of exceeding beauty and great splendour and light. Among them also: there appeared in the sky images of horsemen of fire, flying in the air close to the ground, over Jerusalem and over the whole land of the Jews. Among them also: on the night of the Feast of Pentecost in Jerusalem, the priests heard the sound of a great multitude coming and going in the Temple without their being seen; they only heard their footsteps. Then they heard a great voice saying: "Let us go, let us depart from this House." Among them also: four years before this, a man had appeared in the city who walked like a madman and cried out at the top of his voice, saying: "A voice from the east! A voice from the west! A voice from the four quarters of the world! A voice against Jerusalem! A voice against the Temple! A voice against the fortress! A voice against the cities! A voice against all the people! Woe to Jerusalem! Woe to Jerusalem!" He never ceased from these words, and the people hated him, rebuked him, and deemed him mad. He continued in this state until the enemy surrounded the city (p-347). Then one day, as was his custom, he began to speak, and a stone struck him on the head and he died. And there was found on the wall of the Holy of Holies an ancient stone inscribed: "When the building of the Temple becomes square, a great king will rule over the land of the children of Israel, and will dominate all the earth." Some people said: he is the king of the Children of Israel. The wise men and priests said: rather, it is the Romans. And there was also found an ancient stone inscribed: "When the building of Jerusalem is completed and becomes square, then at that time it will be destroyed." When the siege came and the Antonia was demolished, they blocked up the wall, and so the Temple became square, as will be explained. The greatest of the signs was the fighting among their rebels, the shedding of blood of the elite and the common, burning, and hunger, to such an extent that calamity encompassed them and all the people, and they found no escape, until they came to hate life.

[p. 348] When Titus was freed from the Khawarij (the insurgent factions, lit. "those who went out"), he spent the night in his camp. Then he marched out of Yalu by night and arrived at Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) at dawn. He camped on the summit of the Mount of Olives, which lies to the east of the city of Urshalim (Jerusalem), in order to cut off the valley between himself and the city, so that no one could come out from it toward him without his knowing. He then arranged his army and charged them to cooperate, support one another, stay alert and be cautious, and not to separate from one another. He said: "You are fighting a people whom you have never fought the like of in courage, bravery, endurance in battle, and knowledge of war."

[p. 348 continued] When the Jews saw him, the leaders of the Khawarij, Yuhanan (John), Shim'un (Simon), and Al'azar (Eleazar), agreed not to fight one another, and to unite against the Romans. They gathered, opened the gate of the city, met those of the Romans who were nearby, and fought them. The fighting intensified, and the Romans were defeated. Titus turned them back and encouraged them, so they returned, and a great battle took place between them in which a vast number were killed. The Jews were defeated and withdrew to the wall, and they sent a detachment of their companions, in large numbers, from another direction. They circled behind the Roman camp, while the others advanced from the front, so the Romans were caught between the two forces. A great number of them were killed and they were routed. Titus held firm with a group of his companions, and the affair grew severe until he nearly was killed. His companions said: "Go to the mountain!" But he chose death over defeat, and he continued fighting them until he escaped, after the Jews had overpowered him three times.

When the Jews returned to the city, they broke their covenants and fought one another as they had before, because Yuhanan wanted leadership, while Shim'un and Al'azar refused that. The feast of Passover, which is the Unleavened Bread (al-fatir), arrived, and Yuhanan entered al-Quds (Jerusalem) with his companions on the first day [p. 349]. The people met them with courtesy and were pleased with them, but they stripped off their outer garments and found weapons beneath them. They seized the gates over the people and killed a great number of the priests (kahana) and others, showing no mercy to young or old. Al'azar and Shim'un killed whoever was outside al-Quds from Yuhanan's group. He came out against them, the affair grew severe, and the fighting became continuous.

When Titus learned of this, he advanced toward the city. A group of Jews who were on the wall said to him: "We will open the gate for you on condition that you grant us safe-conduct and relieve us of these Khawarij." But he did not trust them, because of the evil and treachery he had seen from them. Voices rose in the city, because some of them wanted to open the gate for Titus while others prevented it. They hurried to guard the gates and the wall. A group of Romans advanced toward the city, hoping the gate would be opened for them, but the Khawarij pelted them with stones and arrows, and those who had summoned the Romans to enter helped them. Then a group of Jews came out, routed the Romans, inflicted heavy losses on them, pursued them to near their camp, and began to mock them and reproach them for their defeat. Those in the camp wanted to meet them, but Titus prevented them, and his anger toward his companions grew intense. He said: "I am not surprised at the Jews' treachery, but I am surprised at you, with your knowledge of war and your abundant experience. How were you deceived? [p. 350] You went to the city without my command and disobeyed my instruction, and that is why you were defeated. It is not permissible for subjects to disobey the king's order. You know that one of our kings killed his son because he went to war without his command. You deserve death for your disobedience and you are liable for the defeat that befell you." Titus's companions prostrated before him, acknowledged their error, and said: "We will not return to it." He ordered them to level the uneven ground and the depressions around the city and to fill in the wells, so that fighting would be easier for them, and so that the wall could be demolished. They did this, and cut down all the trees and plants around the city. There had been many gardens all around it, in every direction, containing all kinds of trees and fruits, extending for miles. Whoever approached it would see the finest view, but the Romans left nothing of it. Whoever knew those gardens, when he saw them after their destruction, would weep and feel desolate.

The Jews were occupied with their own Khawarij. Shim'un and Al'azar combined against Yuhanan, who had taken al-Quds and had with him eight thousand and four hundred brave men. Shim'un had with him ten thousand Jews and five thousand from Edom, meaning the Christians. The priests and a group of the people of the city were with Al'azar. The people were in the worst condition among these factions. Whenever the Romans prevailed over the city, they united and fought them, but when they repelled them, they returned to their own evil among themselves.

Then Titus brought up the iron ram and other siege engines to demolish the wall. He built great towers of wood, equal in height to the city wall, with rollers beneath them so that men could push them, and fighters could climb onto them. He sent a man from his companions to call them to peace, but one of those on the wall shot him and killed him. The Khawarij reconciled and went out against the Romans, fought them, burned the ram and all those siege engines, drove them back, and returned to the city, fighting among themselves. When Titus learned of this, he pushed the ram against the wall and knocked down a large section of it. Those behind it fled to the second wall. The Romans cleared away the stones that had fallen from the wall so that there would be room for them. The Khawarij reconciled and spread their companions over the sections of the city. The fighting between them and the Romans intensified, both sides fought with determination, and Titus took charge of the battle himself. He came forward, encouraging his companions and promising them wealth and gifts. Shim'un encouraged his own men and called out: "Whoever flees will be killed and his house will be demolished!"

When Titus saw the steadfastness of Shim'un's companions, he turned toward the area of Yuhanan, because it was level and easy. He wanted to batter the second wall, but a man named Qastur [p. 352] called out to him from above the wall: "I ask you, my lord, to have compassion on this city, since the affair is going as you wish." Titus believed his sincerity and halted, and began speaking with him, prolonging the discussion as a ruse so that his companions could burn the ram. Then he asked him to send someone from his companions so they could come to an agreement. Qastur sent to him a man of the notables of the Romans. Qastur said to him: "Come closer so I can tell you what I have, then descend." He threw a rock at him, but missed him and killed a man who was with him. Titus became angry and drove the ram against the second wall, and a large section of it collapsed. Qastur's grief intensified and he killed himself. The Jews hurried forward and prevented the Romans from entering through the breach. They fought them until they drove them back from the first wall, killing a number of them. The fighting between the two sides continued for four days. On the fourth day, a great army from various nations arrived to help Titus against the Jews. The Jews came out as was their custom and fought them, but they had no strength against them and were routed. They entered the third fortress. Titus ordered a halt to the fighting and held off from them for five days. On the fifth day he rode out and advanced close to the wall [p. 353], where he found that Yuhanan, Shim'un, and their companions had come out of the city to burn the ram. Titus greeted them first and addressed them with kindness and gentleness, saying: "You have seen what happened with the destruction of these two walls. The demolition of the third wall is not impossible. You know that you have gained nothing from what you have done during this period, and likewise you will gain nothing by persisting in your stubborn opposition to us. Turn back from this before I demolish this remaining wall, plunder the city, and destroy the Temple (al-Haykal). I do not choose that, nor do I want it. If you return to our obedience, we will treat you with the best of what you have known from us, your safety will continue, and the hardship you are suffering will be removed from you."

[p-354] Yusuf ibn Kariyun (Joseph son of Kariyun) was ordered to draw near to them, to carry the matter with them to the utmost in speech, to call them to peace, and to offer them such assurances and covenants that they would trust him and be at ease with him. So he stood before the gate of the city and said: "Listen to me, O assembly of the Children of Israel, to what I am addressing you with, for I address you only with what benefits you and returns to your good if you accept it. Know that fighting the enemies and resisting them was fitting for you when your lands were prosperous, your armies numerous, and your conditions sound. But now that you have come to this state, through the ruin of the lands, the perishing of the men, the loss of blessings and the disorder of affairs, how can you hope to resist this great, mighty nation, which has conquered kingdoms and peoples and taken control over them? On what, then, do you rely? If you say, 'We rely upon Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, and we hope that He will give us victory, as His custom has been with our fathers,' then you must know that it is He who has given this nation power over you because of your evil deeds and the multitude of your sins, for you have committed the prohibited things, shed blood, defiled the holy sanctuary of Allah, and killed its priests and the righteous of its community unjustly. How, then, can you hope for victory and help from Allah with these shameful deeds? Allah does not give victory to one who disobeys Him. And if you rely on the fortresses, the equipment and the armies, you know that most of all that has gone, and only a little remains. This city has had two of its walls demolished and only one remains, and they are diligent in demolishing it, while you are every day in decline and weakness, and your enemy is increasing in numbers and strength. If you continue in what you are upon, you will perish and not a remnant of you will be left. If you say, 'We choose death over humiliation before the nations and obedience to them,' then you know that our fathers and our forebears, who are the leaders whom we must follow, did not refuse to make peace with the nations who were their neighbors and to accommodate them. Had it been a detestable matter, they would have been the first to detest it, more than you. Our predecessors obeyed the Egyptians for many periods, and the kings of Mosul, the Chaldeans, the Persians, and then the Greeks, who oppressed them, wronged them, and they endured their injustice until Allah permitted their deliverance from them at the hands of the Hasmonean priests. After that they obeyed the kings of Rome up to this point, and they did not regard it as a flaw in their obedience. Likewise, if you obey them, that would be better for you than exposing yourselves to destruction, your blessing to extinction, and your land to ruin, and then finding yourselves, after all that, in greater humiliation than what you dislike. No reasonable person will excuse you in that, and your opinion will not be praised. Moreover, the Romans have continually been good to you: they relieved you of the affair of your enemies, the Greeks, removed their authority from you, and helped you against many of the nations who oppose you, until you overcame them and became dominant over them. So obeying them is more fitting for you than disobeying them. You know that Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, has assigned to every nation a dynasty and an authority, through which He empowers it. When that time ends, its dynasty and authority pass away, and it is humbled before others and submits to those who used to submit to it. [p-356] Allah has extended your hands for a time and given you power over others for an age, then He gave the dynasty and authority to others, and He willed to humble you before them. So if you oppose the will of Allah and do not accept His judgment, you will perish. There is no doubt that Allah wills in this time to raise the Romans and extend their hands, for He has humbled kings before them and granted them victory over the nations, so that those in all regions of the world obey them, including those who are stronger than you in might, more numerous in quantity, and mightier in authority. How, then, do you hope to defeat them while you witness their ascendancy, the strength of their affair, and Allah's help for them, and you see yourselves as being in the opposite condition? A person is not disgraced nor diminished by obeying one who is stronger than him and higher in power, because Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, has made the affair of creation in this world based on some being subordinate to others, some dominating others, and some needing others. Every class submits to one stronger than itself, is humbled before it, and obeys it. This is evident and existing among people in their various strata and among animals in their different kinds, and no one is independent of this, nor does any reasonable person blame it. Since the matter is so, the obedience to the Romans does not diminish you, and the Romans are not the first whom you have obeyed. Your obedience to them has preceded by many years. Now they have approached you in this time with kindness, invited you to peace, offered you safety, guaranteed you good treatment, and shown their concern for your city and your Holy Place. So fear Allah, [p-357] correct your affair, take good care of those of you who remain, and return to what you were upon of obedience to them, so that you may survive, your conditions may be stabilized, and this city and this noble Holy Place may be preserved before this last remaining stronghold is demolished and you perish."

Then the rebels cried out, cursing Yusuf and slandering him, and they pelted him with arrows and stones. So he withdrew a little and spoke to them harshly, saying: "O assembly of rebels, tell me, what has driven you to fight the Romans? If you intend by that to protect Jerusalem from the enemies, then you have already degraded it with sins and defiled it with the many lives you have shed in it unjustly. And if you wish to support the nation and strengthen it, then you are killing it with your own hands and exaggerating in wronging it and harming it. Will the enemies do to you more than what you have done, or will they go further against you than what you have already reached against yourselves? Tell me, when did those of our nation, whether earlier or later, ever defeat those who fought against them, or prevail over their enemies with equipment and numbers without righteousness and piety? Did anyone escape from hardships except by obedience to Allah and by calling upon Him? Did they ever prevail except by Allah's victory for them and His help for them? Did He ever give them victory except when they obeyed Him and feared Him? When they disobeyed Him, He gave their enemies power over them and enabled them over them until they overpowered and humiliated them, and they did not benefit from their numbers and weapons, nor were they able to resist the enemies with their might and strength. You know that Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, has sufficed the righteous in every age against their enemies. Some of them called upon Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, in times of hardship, and He responded to them without war, and manifested great signs in their help and sufficiency, so they attained by that what they could not have attained by their own power and strength. Others fought the enemies and sought help from Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, so He aided them against their enemy and granted them victory over him. Allah did not do the like of this with the disobedient, so that the virtue of the righteous might be manifested. Consider your father Abraham, peace be upon him, when Pharaoh took his wife. Did not Allah strike Pharaoh and his household with a great affliction until he submitted and was broken, and returned Abraham's wife unharmed? Then He treated him well and honored him. Could Abraham, peace be upon him, have achieved that by the sword and fighting, or by righteousness and calling to Allah, [p-359] Exalted and Majestic is He? Likewise Allah did with Isaac, peace be upon him, when Abimelech, king of Philistia, took his wife. You know that Moses, peace be upon him, did not prevail over Pharaoh and the armies of the Egyptians until they perished, and the nation of the Children of Israel was delivered from them, not by war or equipment, but by supplication and Allah's sufficiency for him. When Amalek fought the Children of Israel, did they defeat him except by the supplication and prayer of Moses, peace be upon him? And Joshua son of Nun, peace be upon him, when he crossed the Jordan with the Children of Israel, was in a large host with strength. Did he conquer Jericho by war, or by the wondrous sign of the fall of the fortress? When Achan erred by taking from Jericho some of the spoils that Allah had forbidden to the Children of Israel, did not Allah become angry with the nation because of him, until the people of the city of Ai overcame them while they were few? The Children of Israel, despite their multitude, could not resist them, until Joshua son of Nun, peace be upon him, prayed and called upon Allah, Exalted and Majestic is He, so Allah answered his supplication and gave the Children of Israel victory over Ai and Gideon, when he defeated the army of Midian and Amalek, despite their numbers. [p-360] Did he defeat them except by Allah's help for them? Remember how the great Armenian army was routed from Sebaste by the prayer and supplication of the Prophet Elisha, peace be upon him, when the people of the city had come close to perishing from hunger. Allah cast fear into the hearts of the Armenians, so they fled without battle or fighting, and the people of the city came out and seized their camp, and hunger was removed from them. Remember what Allah did with the wives of the king, Jehoshaphat, when He granted them victory over their enemies through supplication and prayer. You know that Samson, before he erred, was a mighty and victorious warrior. But when he erred, his enemies captured him, and he became humble in their hands, like the lowliest and weakest of men, and they ground him at the mill like female slaves. Likewise Saul, or in another version Talut, the king: when he was obedient to Allah, Exalted, Allah helped him, but when he disobeyed Him, Allah delivered him to his enemies, and they prevailed over him, and he did not benefit from his armies and equipment. Amaziah, when he fought Edom, defeated them and prevailed over them, but when he took their idols and set them up in Jerusalem, [p-361] Allah became angry with him. When Joash, king of the Children of Israel, later fought, he was routed in the most shameful defeat because of Allah's abandonment of him and His withdrawal of help from him. Remember the destruction of the army of Sennacherib, king of Mosul, the great army, without war or fighting, but by the prayer of Hezekiah the king and the prophets, peace be upon them, and their supplication. Take lesson from Zedekiah the king, when he disobeyed the Chaldeans, thinking that he would overcome them with his armies and equipment, and opposed the prophets, peace be upon them, regarding making peace with them. Did he benefit from that? Was not his outcome, and the outcome of the nation, nothing but destruction? This, and other things I have not mentioned to you, shows you Allah's care for the righteous and His abandonment of the wicked, disobedient evildoers."

Thus he addressed them with many eloquent words of this kind. Then he urged them to obey Isfisyanus (Vespasian) in particular, because of his well-known good conduct, and said: "Even if you knew nothing of him except the kindness he has shown me, though I deserved something other than that from him, it would be enough for you. For I was the first to strive against him and I killed a great many of his companions. I knew well that I had opposed what was right, but when I saw you all united in fighting them, and you sent me forth, I did not oppose you. I exerted my utmost effort in advising you, and I held firm in the fortress of Yodanat until my companions were destroyed and the matter overcame me and I had no recourse left. Then I came over to the Romans, and they did not mistreat me; rather, they treated me well, honored me, and pardoned me. I am with them until this end, in what I love. Before I came over to them I had striven to flee to you, but that was not accomplished for me. Now I praise God (Exalted) that He did not make that easy for me, for if I had been with you, I would either have had to share in these deeds of yours, and thus be in error, or oppose you, and you would kill me unjustly. So reflect on what I have addressed to you. Do not suppose that God will give you victory, for you do not deserve that, since you have angered Him. Take as evidence for this the sign of the spring of Silwan, which was nearly dry before these armies came down upon you, but when they descended it gushed forth and became like a river, so that you might know that God (Exalted) wills the aid of your enemies against you. I know that my words will have no effect on you, so that what God has decreed of the destruction of this city and the ruin of this glorious Holy House may be fulfilled. For this reason your hearts have hardened and become like stones, indeed harder and firmer than stones, for water may affect a stone if its pouring upon it continues, but many admonitions do not affect you, nor do your hearts soften or break. But I have reached the limit in what is incumbent on me of advising you. So accept my counsel, and have compassion on this glorious Holy House which the sanctified prophets and the great kings built, for the continuance of your might, the firmness of your affairs, are bound to its continuance and its prosperity. If it is ruined, you will have no might, no good fortune, and no dominion. So accept what the son of the king (Titus) has offered you of safety, trust in his covenant and in the goodness he has guaranteed, and I stand as guarantor for you concerning it. Even if you accuse me of deceiving you and of wanting to help the Romans against you, you know that my father, my mother, my noble wife dear to me, and my children are with you. So if after your peace with him there appears to you from Titus anything you dislike, then kill them and kill me; for I have granted you their lives and my own on that condition."

Then Yusuf wept intensely. Titus was listening to his speech, and he was moved by it. He ordered the release of those among the captives who were in his army, and he allowed them to go wherever they wished. Most of the people of the city then inclined to obey Titus, but the Kharijites (Khawarij) prevented them, appointed men to guard the city gates, and ordered those guards to kill anyone who tried to leave. When the siege was prolonged, hunger became severe. The Kharijites searched people's houses, plundered their food, and killed whoever withheld it from them. So the people were dying of hunger in the city, and whoever tried to go out to the outskirts of the city to take some of the plants of the earth, the Kharijites killed him, and if he managed to go out, the Romans killed him. This destroyed them. Whenever Titus heard of this, he was moved with pity for them and sought to win them over, but his conciliation only increased the Kharijites in harshness, and they addressed him with foul words so that he would desist, lest the people incline toward him. When he saw this, he earnestly set about destroying the third wall, to free the people from the Kharijites. He divided his army into four divisions and set up battering rams on the four sides. The Kharijites came out against them and fought them a fierce battle, and they killed a great many of the Romans. They had designated four of their most valiant men to burn the battering rams when the enemy was occupied with fighting, and they continued fighting them until they accomplished what they wanted, and they burned the rams and all their equipment. The Romans saw the courage and might of the Jews, which terrified them, so they fled. Titus turned them back and began to encourage them, saying: "Are you not ashamed that the Jews should defeat you after we have gained the upper hand over them, and have demolished two of the city's walls, and only one wall remains, and most of them have perished, and they have no one to help them? We have abundant armies, and with us are many peoples helping us against them." Then he ordered them to cease fighting them until they died of hunger. So they seized all the roads of the city, and the matter became extremely straitened for them, and hunger grew severe. No one could grind wheat for fear of it being plundered, nor could anyone bake bread lest the smoke expose him. Whoever had something would eat wheat and flour raw, and many people died. The living were preoccupied with themselves, so they did not bury their dead. Sometimes a family would take its dead and throw it into a well, then cast itself down after it to die. Some would dig a grave for himself and then lie down in it until he died. The streets filled with corpses, and the Kharijites would throw them from the wall into the eastern valley. When Titus saw them, he was grieved and pitied them. In Jerusalem there was a woman of the people of wealth, whose origin was from a city in the region of the Jordan. When the strife grew great there, she moved, among those who moved to Jerusalem, with all her slaves and all her possessions. She had only one small son, whom she loved intensely. When the famine intensified and the Kharijites plundered everything she had, her situation became severe. Her son was writhing from hunger, and as hunger increased for her, and what pained her heart of her son's writhing, she wanted to kill her son to eat him. So she remained bewildered, not knowing to which of the two courses she should commit herself: whether to kill her beloved son with her own hand, which is among the greatest and most abominable of things, or to endure what she saw of affliction for him and herself. Patience had abandoned her and endurance was gone. Then hunger increased further, and her discernment left her. She said: "O my son, my only one! I used to hope you would live until you were good to me, and I feared you would die before me and I would be bereaved by your death. Would that I had been bereaved of you and had buried you and reckoned you with God. And now, O my son, calamity has encircled us and we are certain of destruction. The living no longer hopes for life, and the dead are not buried. You and I are both doomed. If you die, my son, no one will bury you, and you will be like others whom dogs and the birds of the sky have eaten. I have decided to kill you so that you may rest from what you are in, then I will eat you, and make my belly, which carried you, a grave for you, and satisfy my hunger with you. That will be in place of the goodness you showed me, which I hoped for, and you will obtain great reward thereby, and it will be a disgrace upon these Kharijites who brought us into this affliction, and an increase in the wrath of God upon them. It will be remembered throughout the passage of time, and generations after us will speak of it, and people of understanding will take a lesson from it." Then she seized her son with one hand and took the knife in the other, and she was like one out of her mind, [p-367] and she turned her face away from him so that she would not see him, and she struck him with the knife, and he died. Then she took from him and roasted him and ate him. When the Kharijites smelled the scent of that meat, they rushed upon her and said to her: "Where did you get this meat? And why did you keep it to yourself apart from us?" She said: "I am not one who prefers herself over you. Sit down." So she brought the table, and brought out what remained of her son's body, and said: "This is my son, the dearest of people to me. I killed him with my own hand because of the extremity of hunger, and I ate some of his flesh. This is the remainder of his body, which I set aside for you. So eat and be satisfied, and do not be more merciful to my son than I was. Do not let your hearts weaken from this, for it is shameful for brave men like you that a woman should be stronger of heart than you, and you are more deserving of being content with this from me, because you are the ones who brought the affliction upon us until we reached this extent." Then she raised her voice weeping, sobbing, and wailing over her son. When they saw that, it terrified them, and they went out in panic. Her story spread, and the people were greatly disturbed, and they were certain of the truth of the threat that had come from God beforehand. The Kharijites were broken by this and were appalled, and they allowed the people to leave, so at that time a great number went out.

When this reached Titus, he was appalled by it, and his fear of God (Exalted) intensified. He raised his hand to heaven and said: "O God, You are the Knower of hidden things and the One who sees into secrets and intentions. You know that I did not come to this city to harm its people, and the matter of this woman has grieved me, so do not hold me accountable for it. Pursue these Kharijites, take vengeance on them, grant me victory over them, and do not give them respite." He ordered kindness to those Jews who came out to him, for many of them could not open their mouths, many died after eating food, and children and others would snatch bread when they saw it and gobble it down without reason, and when they ate they died. Then Titus said to Yusuf ibn Kiryun: "What is the remedy for these people so that they do not die?" He said: "They should be given milk and thin broth for some days until their intestines soften, then food after that." So he did that, and a group of them was saved. The Romans advanced to the third wall to demolish it, and Yuhanan, Shimʿun, and their companions came out against them, despite the harm they were in, and they fought them fiercely and killed a group of them. Titus then ordered the battering ram to be brought against the wall, and it was pushed against it at night, and it was demolished. The Romans shouted a mighty shout of takbir, and the Jews shouted takbir from inside the city. The Romans did not dare to enter the city, [p-369] but when they woke in the morning, there was a new wall facing the breach, which the Jews had built that night while standing guard over it. The Romans were astonished by this and despaired of conquest. Titus said: "This is green (unseasoned) and has not hardened, and when the ram strikes it, it will collapse quickly." So the Romans climbed the wall they had demolished, and the Jews stood on the new wall, and the fighting intensified. The Jews defeated them after killing many of them. The Romans became weary and resolved to depart. Titus gathered his companions and said: "Know that everyone who does a work, his aim is toward its end, and therefore he endures fatigue to reach what he wants. Often the last part of a work is harder than its beginning. If he abandons it, his effort is lost and his work remains incomplete, of no benefit."

He struck examples for them in this matter. Then he said: "You have endured the fight against this people and have prevailed over them to this extent, until their leaders and tyrants have perished, their fortresses have been destroyed, and they have been worn down by hunger and the sword. Only a small remnant remains of them, like the dead. If you now withdraw, you will have wasted your toil, and you will have aided yourselves against yourselves, and you will have humiliated them [p. 370] in the eyes of everyone who hears of you. Had you withdrawn from them before this, it would have been better for you. But now there is no excuse for you in your inability to fight a people whose distress and hunger have reached this point. If you turn back from them, everyone will covet you, and everyone who fears you will become bold against you. Why do you not take the Jews as an example in patience and courage, despite the annihilation of their men, the gathering of hardships upon them, and the cutting off of their hope? Their patience is either from hope of victory, or from disdain of defeat, or from desire for the lasting of their renown. You are more entitled to this than they are, so that you may repel shame from yourselves. Moreover, you were patient in the days of Tiberius Caesar in fighting this people, and you resolved not to turn back from them until you had won. Then when Vespasian (Isfisyanus) took power, who is braver than Tiberius and greater in might, you wished to turn back from them before you had won. So what excuse do you have?" When they heard this, they held firm.

Then a group of them went out at night, climbed up through that breach, and entered the city, and they shouted "Allahu akbar." The Jews awoke, for they had slept from the length of their exhaustion and distress, and each one remained in his place. Titus went to his companions and stood at the wall until morning. Then the Jews fled to Jerusalem, and the Romans pursued them, and they fought in the outer courtyard. There was nothing but swords because of the narrowness of the place. There was between them a fighting that had not occurred before, since all were facing one another, for they had come to a place where there was no hope of safety except through sincerity in fighting. All of them were infantry. The war between them grew fierce, their voices and clamor rose until they were heard from afar, and many were killed on both sides. At last the Jews gained the upper hand and drove the Romans out near the quarter of the day. Titus ordered the demolition of the wall of a place adjoining Jerusalem called Antonia, so that there would be room for his companions. When that was demolished, the wall of Jerusalem was breached and the approach to it became easy. The Jews hurried and built it up, and included it within Jerusalem, so that it became square. This was the fulfillment of what they had seen written before on the ancient stone mentioned earlier: "When the building of Jerusalem is completed and it becomes square, then the House of the Maqdis will be destroyed." The Jews had forgotten this, but when they saw it they remembered, and they knew that the term had been completed and that it would be destroyed.

The day of this great war was the feast of Pentecost (al-'Ansarah, the feast of the Christians). Titus drew near to Jerusalem and spoke to them, encouraging them to make peace so that they might be free to worship on this feast, and he promised them kindness. He said: "You know that your king Bahnya, when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged him and he went out to him seeking safe conduct, benefited by that, and benefited his people and his land, so they were saved. And you know that King Zedekiah, when he persisted in fighting Nebuchadnezzar and did not make peace with him as the prophets had commanded, destroyed the city and the nation, and wronged himself and them. So your path is to take warning from these two, and to be guided by the more righteous of their deeds and the more praiseworthy of their outcomes. So accept my advice, be content with what has occurred," and he promised to pardon all that had preceded and to treat them well. He prolonged his speech.

Yusuf ibn Kariyun was having mercy on them and weeping bitterly. Then Yusuf said to them: "I am not surprised at the ruin of this city, for I know that its term has ended. But I am amazed at you, while you read the book of the prophet Daniel, peace be upon him, and know what he mentioned of the invalidity of the sacrifices and the absence of the Messiah priest, and yet you do not submit, nor do you humble yourselves before God, nor do you yield to the one whom God has set over you." The rebels did not accept, nor did they turn back, except that a group of the priests and leaders managed to go out to the Romans, and he granted them safe conduct and treated them well. The rebels then prevented those who remained, and they seized the roads. The Jews wept and complained that the rebels were preventing them from leaving. So the rebels intended to kill them, and the Romans hastened to rescue them. They attacked Jerusalem and fought them a fierce battle. The Romans were defeated, and the defeat drove them to the innermost part of Jerusalem, the Holy of Holies (Qudas al-Aqdas), where the Jews killed them. Titus then selected thirty thousand from his army and ordered them to enter the courtyard of Jerusalem to fight them, and he himself wished to enter with them, but his companions prevented him and said: "Stand at an elevated place so that your companions' hearts will be strengthened, and they will exert their utmost effort in fighting. Do not risk yourself and us." Their opinion agreed on a night attack. The Jews learned of this and did not sleep that night. When morning came, the Jews spread out at the gates of the courtyard of Jerusalem, and they kept fighting the Romans for seven days. They killed a large number of them and drove them away from Jerusalem. Then Titus ordered his companions to refrain from them so that hunger would destroy them. Near Jerusalem there was a great palace built by Solomon son of David, peace be upon them both. Later the kings of the Second Temple added a high story to it of fine wood and lined all its walls with wood. Then they smeared all the wood in it with naphtha, sulfur, and pitch. Then they hid a man among them who would set fire to places of that wood when the Romans entered. There was a hidden door in it leading to another place, which no one would notice except one who knew it. Then they went to the Roman camp at night, while they were in Jerusalem, and skirmished with them. A great number of Romans gathered against them, and they fought them for a while, then they retreated and entered this palace. The Romans entered after them but found none of them. They climbed to the upper story, and the Jew who had hidden came out and mingled with them and set fire to those places. The fire blazed on all sides of it. The Romans hurried to the door, but found the Jews had blocked it with their swords, so they perished. Among them were a number of Roman notables, so the Romans feared the Jews and did not feel safe that they might devise some other plot against them. So they left Jerusalem and the city and returned to their camp. Titus then ordered the roads to be secured and a tight siege imposed on them so that hunger would destroy them, and most of them died. Many of the rebels came out to Titus, and he killed them. Then the Romans entered the House of God and found no one to resist them. Titus had emphatically instructed his companions not to burn Jerusalem. But the leaders of his companions said to him: "If you do not burn it, you will not be able to subdue the Jews, for they will keep fighting as long as it remains standing. But when it is burned, their glory will be gone, their hearts will be broken, and they will have nothing left to fight for." He said: "Do not burn it unless I order you." There was a gate on his route, covered with silver plates, and it was locked. Some of the Romans burned it in order to take the silver. When it burned, they found the way to the Greater Jerusalem, so they entered it, carried their idols, and set them up in it. Then a group of the Jews who remained came out at night to those in Jerusalem and killed them. When this reached Titus, he came to Jerusalem and killed most of the Jews he found in it, and those who remained of them fled to Mount Zion. The next day the Romans burned the gates of the Holy of Holies, which were covered with gold. When they fell, they shouted "Allahu akbar" and cried out with a great cry. Titus came hastening to prevent its burning, but he did not succeed. It is said that he shouted until his voice gave out. When he knew the matter had escaped his control, he entered to look at it before it burned. When he saw its beauty and splendor, he was bewildered and amazed, and said: "Truly, this glorious House ought to be the House of God, the God of heaven, the dwelling of His majesty and light. The Jews have every right to fight for it and to be zealous for it. The nations were right, and did well in what they used to do of honoring and glorifying this House and bringing gifts to it. It is greater than the temple of Rome and all the temples of the nations that we have seen and whose reports have reached us. I did not intend to burn it, but they did it through their evil and obstinacy." Those priests who remained, when they saw the fire, fought the Romans for it. When they knew they were unable to repel them, they said: "We do not wish to remain after it." So they threw themselves into the fire and perished. Then those Jews who remained went to all the grand palaces and fine houses in the city, and they burned them with all their treasures and implements. The burning of Jerusalem occurred on the tenth day of the fifth month, which is Ab, and this corresponds to the day on which the Chaldeans burned the First House.

When the next day came, a Jewish man claiming to be a prophet appeared, and he said to them: "Know that this Jerusalem will soon be rebuilt as it was, without humans building it, but by the power of God (may He be exalted). So persist in what you are doing, fighting the Romans and refusing to obey them." A group gathered around him and they fought, but the Romans overcame them and killed them, all of them, and they killed many of the common Jews and their weak ones, who had had mercy on him before. Yohanan and Shim'un corresponded with Titus, asking him for safe conduct. He said: "I asked you for this before, but now you are in my grip, and I have no excuse before God or anyone among the people for sparing you both."

They then descended by night toward Jerusalem with their companions, and they killed two Roman commanders. Titus ordered the killing of those Jews who remained in the city, including those whom he had shown mercy. When the companions of Shim'un [p. 377] saw this, they feared for themselves, so they sent to Titus asking him to grant them safe conduct. Shim'un killed their leaders, and the rest fled to Titus, who granted them safe conduct, and he restrained his companions from those Jews who remained in the city. Then Shim'un and Yohanan fled from Mount Zion to a place where they hid. Thus Titus completed his conquest of the whole land, and he demolished the wall of Mount Zion. When their concealment lasted long and hunger pressed hard upon them, they came out to Titus, and he killed them both. Then he set out toward Rome, and with him were the captives and the spoils. Whenever he halted at a stopping place, he would throw a group of the rebels he had captured to the beasts that were with him, until he annihilated them.

Ol'azar, when he saw the corruption of Shim'un and his killing of those Jews who had no guilt, knew that there was no deliverance for them from the calamity. So he left before the Romans conquered the city and stayed in some places. When Titus departed, he went to the village of Masira and rebuilt its fortress. Titus heard of him while he was in Antioch, so he sent back one of his commanders to besiege him. When he saw destruction, he called his companions to kill those dependents behind them and to fight to the death, so that they might die honorably. They agreed to this, and they fought until they were all killed. Glory be to the Mighty, the Severe, the Doer of what He wills.

(p-378) When that was over, it was as if it were said: "Will there not be a return for this time, like the first?" So He, glorified and exalted, gave them hope with His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾; that is, He who has accustomed you to His kindness; ﴿that He will have mercy upon you﴾; so He will accept your repentance; and honor you. Then He alarmed them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you return﴾; that is, to disobedience a third time, and whatever comes after it; ﴿We will return﴾; that is, with what you know of Our might; to Our punishment of you in this world; and they did return more than once, as the discourse indicates, even though it is in the form of a conditional, so that the distinction between the speech of the learned and others would become clear. And to this His saying in the Torah points, after what has passed: "When all these words have come upon you, both the blessing and the curse which I have set before you, and you call them to mind among all the nations where the LORD your God has driven you, and you return to the LORD your God and obey His voice according to all that I command you this day, you and your children, with all your heart and with all your soul, then the LORD your God will restore your captivity and have compassion on you, and will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are in the farthest parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you, and from there He will bring you back. The LORD your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it; and He will make you more prosperous and more numerous than your fathers. And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your descendants, to love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live" (p-379) "and fear the LORD your God with all your heart and all your soul, so that He may relieve you and bless you, and the LORD your God will bring all these curses upon your enemies and those who hate you and persecuted you." ﴿And We have made﴾; that is, after that, by Our majesty; ﴿Hell﴾; into which you will be cast with scowling and aversion; ﴿a prison for the disbelievers﴾; and this apparent description stands in place of a pronoun, to show that the ruling is attached to it in a firm manner; this applies to them and to others; and it indicates that they will return to corruption, and that among them are those who believe and those who disbelieve; ﴿a prison﴾; that is, a confinement that restricts them to the utmost restriction; and it is related from al-Hasan that "ḥaṣīr" is that which is spread out and laid down; so the meaning is that He makes it their bed.

ولَمّا ثَبَتَ أنَّ كِتابَ مُوسى - عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ - الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ فِيما بَيْنَ مِصْرَ وبَيْتِ المَقْدِسِ في تِلْكَ المُدَّةِ المُتَطاوِلَةِ؛ هو هُدًى لِبَنِي إسْرائِيلَ؛ صادِقُ الوَعْدِ والوَعِيدِ فِيما قُضِيَ فِيهِ إلَيْهِمْ مِن أمْرِهم وأمْرِبَيْتِ المَقْدِسِ؛ مِن تَرْقِيَةِ حالِ مَن أطاعَهُ؛ وإعْلائِهِمْ؛ وأخْذِ مَن عاداهُمْ؛ ومِن تَعْكِيسِ أحْوالِ العُصاةِ مَرَّةً بَعْدَ أُخْرى بِتَسْلِيطِ الأعْداءِ عَلَيْهِمْ بِالقَتْلِ؛ والأسْرِ؛ [p-380] والنَّهْبِ؛ وتَخْرِيبِ البِلادِ؛ تَنْبِيهًا عَلى أنَّ طاعَةَ اللَّهِ تَجْلِبُ كُلَّ خَيْرٍ وكَرامَةٍ؛ ومَعْصِيَتَهُ تُوجِبُ كُلُّ بَلِيَّةٍ؛ كَما كَشَفَ عَنْهُ الزَّمانُ عَلى ما هو مَعْرُوفٌ مِن تَوارِيخِ اليَهُودِ وغَيْرِها؛ لاحَ أنَّ القُرْآنَ يَزِيدُ عَلَيْهِ في كُلِّ مَعْنًى حَسَنٍ؛ وأمْرٍ شَرِيفٍ؛ فِيما أتى بِهِ مِنَ الوُعُودِ الصّادِقَةِ؛ والأحْكامِ المُحْكَمَةِ؛ والمَعانِي الفائِقَةِ في النُّظُومِ العَذْبَةِ الرّائِقَةِ؛ مَعَ الإعْجازِ عَنِ الإتْيانِ بِآيَةٍ مِن مِثْلِهِ لِجَمِيعِ الإنْسِ والجانِّ؛ بِنِسْبَةِ ما زادَ المَسِيرُ المُحَمَّدِيُّ إلى بَيْتِ المَقْدِسِ - الَّذِي أراهُ فِيهِ مِن آياتِهِ - عَلى المَسِيرِ المُوسَوِيِّ الَّذِي آتاهُ فِيهِ الكِتابَ؛ فَقالَ - في جَوابِ مَن كَأنَّهُ قالَ: قَدْ عُلِمَ أنَّ كِتابَ مُوسى - عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ - الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ في مَسِيرِهِ لِقَصْدِ مَحَلِّ المَسْجِدِ الأقْصى قَيِّمٌ في الهِدايَةِ والوُعُودِ الصّادِقَةِ؛ فَما حالُ كِتابِ مُحَمَّدٍ - صَلّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وعَلى آلِهِ وسَلَّمَ - الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ مِنهُ في سَبَبِ مَسِيرِهِ إلَيْهِ في ذَلِكَ؟ -: ﴿إنَّ هَذا القُرْآنَ﴾؛ أيْ: الجامِعَ لِكُلِّ حَقٍّ؛ والفارِقَ بَيْنَ كُلِّ مُلْتَبِسٍ؛ ﴿يَهْدِي﴾

ولَمّا كانَ صاحِبُ الذَّوْقِ السَّلِيمِ يَجِدُ لِحَذْفِ المَوْصُوفِ هِزَّةً ورَوْعَةً؛ لِما يَجِدُ مِنَ الفَخامَةِ بِإبْهامِهِ؛ لا يَجِدُها عِنْدَ ذِكْرِهِ وإيضاحِهِ؛ قالَ: ﴿لِلَّتِي﴾ [p-381] أيْ: لِلطَّرائِقِ؛ والأحْوالِ؛ والسُّنَنِ الَّتِي ﴿هِيَ أقْوَمُ﴾؛ مِن كُلِّ طَرِيقَةٍ؛ وسُنَّةٍ؛ وحالٍ؛ دَعا إلَيْها كِتابٌ مِنَ الكُتُبِ السَّماوِيَّةِ؛ أمّا في الصُّورَةِ فَبِاعْتِبارِ ما عَلا بِهِ مِنَ البَيانِ؛ وأمّا في الوُعُودِ؛ فَبِاعْتِبارِ العُمُومِ لِجَمِيعِ الخَلْقِ في الدّارَيْنِ؛ وأمّا في الأُصُولِ فَبِتَصْرِيفِ الأمْثالِ؛ وتَقْرِيبِ الوَسائِلِ؛ وحَسْمِ مَوادِّ الشُّبَهِ؛ وإيضاحِ وُجُوهِ الدَّلائِلِ؛ وأمّا الفُرُوعُ فَبِاعْتِبارِ الأحْسَنِيَّةِ تارَةً في السُّهُولَةِ؛ والخِفَّةِ؛ وتارَةً في غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ - كَما هو واضِحٌ عِنْدَ مَن تَأمَّلَ ما بَيْنَ الأمْرَيْنِ.

ولَمّا انْقَسَمَ النّاسُ إلى مُهْتَدٍ بِهِ؛ وضالٍّ؛ أتْبَعَ - سُبْحانَهُ - ذَلِكَ بَيانَهُ؛ وكانَ التَّعْبِيرُ عَنْ حالِهِما بِالبُشْرى في قَوْلِهِ (تَعالى): ﴿ويُبَشِّرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾؛ أيْ: الرّاسِخِينَ في هَذا الوَصْفِ؛ ولِهَذا قَيَّدَهُمْ؛ بَيانًا لَهُمْ؛ بِقَوْلِهِ (تَعالى): ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾؛ يُصَدِّقُونَ إيمانَهم بِأنَّهم ﴿يَعْمَلُونَ﴾؛ أيْ: عَلى سَبِيلِ التَّجْدِيدِ؛ والِاسْتِمْرارِ؛ والبِناءِ عَلى العِلْمِ؛ ﴿الصّالِحاتِ﴾؛ مِنَ التَّقْوى؛ والإحْسانِ؛ ﴿أنَّ لَهُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: جَزاءً لَهُمْ؛ في ظاهِرِهِمْ؛ وبَواطِنِهِمْ؛ ﴿أجْرًا كَبِيرًا﴾؛ إشارَةً إلى صَلاحِ هَذِهِ الأُمَّةِ؛ وثَباتِهِمْ عَلى دِينِهِمْ؛ وأنَّهُ لا يَزالُ أمْرُهم ظاهِرًا؛ كَما كانَ إنْذارُ كِتابِ مُوسى - عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ - قَوْمَهُ إشارَةً إلى إفْسادِهِمْ؛ وتَبْدِيلِهِمْ دِينَهم.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 10:

When He had given them good news of what is theirs in themselves, He followed it with what is theirs concerning their enemies. So He (Exalted) said: (p-382) ﴿And that﴾; i.e., and He gives good news also to the believers that ﴿those who do not believe﴾; i.e., faith does not renew itself among them ﴿in the Hereafter﴾; in reality or figuratively; the consequence of which is that they do not do righteous deeds in reality, because they do not engage in them; or figuratively, by building them on something other than the foundation of faith. He expressed the provision (al-'atad) with a mocking tone toward them, so He (Exalted) said: ﴿We have prepared﴾; i.e., We have readied and made ready what is in the utmost goodness, nobility and suitability, as a true promise that never fails in any way; and it is, along with that, regarded by Us, owing to Our greatness; ﴿for them﴾; from Us, through the mediation of the believers, or without mediation. When the enemies looked forward to this promise with the eagerness of one who is pleased and delighted, He came to them, in explaining it, with what unsettles their hearts, in the manner of the saying "Their greeting among them is a painful blow," and it greatly gladdened the hearts of the allies; so He (Exalted) said: ﴿a painful punishment﴾; for there is no higher or more delightful good news for those of lofty resolve than retribution against their opponents. Thus the excellence of one Book over another is like the excellence of one going away over another going away. He omitted the believers who do not do righteous deeds, for the completeness of the glad tidings, by indicating that they are so few in this noble community that they are scarcely to be found.

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned what His speech contains of calling to the most upright (al-aqwam), He followed it with the crookedness (i'wijaj) that is in man, which drives him to deviate from holding fast to the upright sacred laws (shara'i') (sharia: the divine law) and to rush into what has no benefit. This is a warning about the need for patient deliberation (ta'anni) in considering what the self calls him to, and in weighing it by the standard of the Law. So He, exalted, said: ﴿And man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good﴾.

The omission of its waw, which is the lam of the verb, is an error in all the mushafs, and there is no reason in Arabic grammar for omitting it in pronunciation. It indicates that he calls down evil because of his foolishness and lack of intellect, though he does not want evil to prevail over him. By omitting what has the meaning of elevation and exaltation according to the people of God, I have pointed to this. It also indicates that the end of his action is destruction, until God overtakes him. I have already mentioned the rule of pausing (waqf) on it and on similar words in Surat "al-Qamar."

﴿Al-insan﴾ (man): that is, in a state of anger and the like, against himself and against those he loves, because of his familiarity with himself and his forgetfulness of what would set him right.

﴿bil-sharr﴾ (for evil): that is, he calls upon his Lord and humbly beseeches Him because evil has befallen him.

﴿du'a'ahu﴾ (his supplication): that is, like his supplication ﴿bil-khayr﴾ (for good): that is, for the attainment of good for himself and for those he loves.

Then He drew attention to the disposition that is the source of this, saying, exalted is He: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾: that is, this kind (of creature), with its little reflection, being occupied with looking at its own inclination (atfiyya) and taking delight in itself, is by nature disposed to this. ﴿'ajula﴾ (hasty): that is, excessively hasty, rushing to seek everything that occurs to his heart and comes to his mind, without deliberating over it with the deliberation of one who sees clearly and does not wish to place anything except in its most fitting place. Therefore he seeks punishment for himself in mockery and for others in order to be healed.

(p. 384) Haste (al-'ajala) is seeking a thing at a time other than its proper time, when it is not permissible to advance it. As for speed (al-sur'a), it is doing a thing at the beginning of its proper time, which is more fitting for it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 12:

When the attribute of exaltedness belonging to His attribute (exalted is He) was established, and the attribute of lowliness belonging to the human being, He followed it with what belongs to His acts (exalted is He) of perfection, mentioning what is most upright of the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood in the two worlds, the higher and the lower. Then [He mentioned] what belongs to human acts of crookedness, following their nature, or of goodness, through the granting of success by the Subtle, the Bestower. So He said (exalted is He), explaining what He bestowed upon them of the blessings of this world after He had bestowed upon them the blessings of religion: ﴿And We made﴾; that is, by the greatness We possess; ﴿the night and the day two signs﴾; indicating the completeness of knowledge and the comprehensiveness of power. The sign of the night is like the ambiguous verses (mutashabihat, those whose meaning is not immediately clear), and the sign of the day is like the firm verses (muhkamat, those whose meaning is clear and definite). Just as the purpose of the obligation is not complete except by mentioning the firm and the ambiguous, so too time cannot be benefited from except by these two signs. ﴿So We effaced﴾ (p-385) that is, by Our dazzling greatness; ﴿the sign of the night﴾; by annihilating the light, so that by it visible things are not seen, just as writing is not seen when it is erased. ﴿And We made﴾; that is, by Our greatness; ﴿the sign of the day﴾; and since it was at the utmost of brightness, by which everyone who has sight sees, He attributed seeing to it as an intensification, so He said: ﴿giving sight﴾; that is, by the sun, which He made luminous in itself. Thus this deficient world is never free from transition from light to darkness and from darkness to light, just as for the human being, with his haste that his nature calls him to and his deliberation that his intellect calls him to, there is transition from deficiency to perfection and from perfection to deficiency. Likewise the moon, which is less than the sun, is so. Then He mentioned some of the benefits that follow from this, saying (exalted is He): ﴿that you may seek﴾; that is, that you may seek eagerly; ﴿bounty from your Lord﴾; that is, the One who does good to you through them: by the light of this at one time, and by the return of that at another; ﴿and that you may know﴾; by distinguishing this from that; ﴿the number of years﴾; that is, without need for calculation, because the two luminaries indicate the turning of the year merely by their movement.

And since the two also indicate the reckoning of risings and settings, increase and decrease, and other occurrences, for one who looks closely and goes deep in reflection, (p-386) He said (exalted is He): ﴿and the reckoning﴾; that is, its kind. We have detailed them for that purpose in this perfected manner, with increase and decrease, and the changing of states at known times, according to an order that does not deviate over the length of time by the weight of an atom, nor loosen by the measure of a hair, until God wills the ruin of the world and the annihilation of creation, and He reduces all of that to nothing in the swiftest time and the nearest moment. Were it not for their alternation, the times would be mixed up and affairs would be disrupted. ﴿And everything﴾ other than them, of what you need in your religion or your worldly life; ﴿We have detailed it﴾; that is, by Our greatness, and We removed its ambiguity. He emphasized the matter to alert to the completeness of power and that nothing that He wills is beyond His ability, so He said (exalted is He): ﴿in detail﴾. So look with your eyes and your insight, and examine both your open and your hidden affairs; you will find a matter perfected and an order firmly established: ﴿Then return the gaze twice; the gaze will return to you humbled and weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 4].

Since this matter is extremely subtle, He followed it with something even more subtle and more striking in terms of power and knowledge, concerning the details of the circumstances of human beings, indeed of every responsible person, some of which are connected to others, before He created them. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿And every person﴾; that is, whoever has in his nature movement and agitation; ﴿We have fastened﴾; that is, by Our greatness; ﴿his bird﴾; that is, his deed which We have decreed for him, of good and evil. Perhaps He expressed it by "bird" (ṭā'ir) because they used to undertake or refrain from important matters of their affairs only by means of the bird, saying: "The bird has gone for so-and-so with such-and-such."

﴿around his neck﴾; that is, the place where necklaces and the like are worn as adornment, and where shackles and the like are placed as disgrace; a fastening from which he cannot be freed from any part of it, just as he cannot free himself from the neck. This is as We imposed on the Children of Israel what We decreed to them in the Book; so it came to be as We said, while they knew that it was in a bad state, yet they could not guard against it or be separated from it. Thus, nothing can appear in eternity except what was decreed in pre-eternity: "The pen has dried with what is to be."

﴿And We will bring forth﴾; that is, by what We possess of greatness, comprehensiveness of knowledge, and perfection of power; ﴿for him on the Day of Resurrection﴾; that is, the Day which must necessarily come into being; ﴿a book﴾, containing everything he did; ﴿which he will find﴾ in the state of being ﴿spread open﴾, which Our guardian angels write down each day. Then, when they ascend, they compare what is in it with what We had inscribed long ago in the Preserved Tablet, and they find it exactly as it is, with no discrepancy in it at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 14:

When he meets his book on the Day of Presentation, it will be said to him: ﴿Read your book.﴾ You yourself, not bound by what anyone else reads. ﴿Sufficient﴾ — and he confirmed the agent by adding the particle bi-: so He (exalted is He) said: ﴿Yourself today is sufficient as a reckoner against you.﴾ That is, throughout this entire day, in which the veils are lifted and all matters become manifest; ﴿as a reckoner against you﴾, that is, a thorough reckoner. For you will be given the ability to read it, whether you were unlettered or a reader; and you will see in it neither addition nor deficiency, and you will not be able to deny a single letter of it. If your tongue denies it, your limbs will bear witness against you. Oh, what a dazzling power, what an overwhelming might, and what manifest justice!

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 15:

When what has passed (the preceding discourse) had yielded, by necessary implication, the meaning of what We said to the Children of Israel, "If you do good..." (the verse), it applies to every person among them and among others. That is His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Whoever is guided﴾, by following the guidance, ﴿then he is guided only for his own soul﴾, because its reward does not exceed him; ﴿and whoever goes astray﴾, by turning away from what We have sent down of clarity, ﴿then he strays only to his own loss﴾, because its punishment is upon him and does not pass beyond him. ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, meaning: whatever bearer it may be, ﴿the burden of another﴾, so that he might lighten it for her. Rather, for every recompense there is its deed, which does not extend beyond its doer to another. So We reward whoever is guided, and We punish whoever goes astray. ﴿And We would not be ones who punish﴾, meaning: in spite of Our greatness, ﴿anyone﴾, ﴿until We send﴾, meaning: a sending that befits Our greatness, ﴿a messenger﴾. So whoever is reached by his call, then opposes his command and is arrogant toward following him, We punish him with what he deserves. This matter has been established by the sending of Adam (peace be upon him) and those after him of the noble prophets (peace and blessings be upon them) among all nations, as He (Exalted) said: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾ [al-Nahl: 36] ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. (p-389) Their call to God (Exalted) had spread, covered the regions, and become well known. Look at the saying of the Quraysh, who had not been visited by a prophet after Isma'il (peace be upon him): ﴿We have not heard of this in the latter religion﴾ [Sad: 7]; for it conveys that they had heard of it in the earlier religion. Thus whoever is reached by the call of any one of them in any way, but falls short in seeking it out, is a disbeliever deserving of punishment. So do not be deceived by the saying of many people regarding the salvation of the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah), together with the report of the Prophet (may God bless him and his family and grant them peace) that their fathers who passed away in the Jahiliyyah are in the Fire, and that the dung beetle that rolls dung is better than them, and other reports of this kind. The Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Halimi, one of the eminent Shafi'is and great leaders of Islam (may God be pleased with them), said at the beginning of his Minhaj, in the chapter on the one who has not been reached by the call: "We have said that whoever among them is a rational, discerning person, who sees and reflects but does not hold any religion, is a disbeliever. For although he may not have heard the call of our Prophet (may God bless him and his family and grant them peace), there is no doubt that he heard the call of one of the prophets who came before him (may God bless him and his family and grant them peace), despite their great number, the long durations of their calls, the abundance of those who believed in them and followed them, and those who disbelieved in them and opposed them. (p-390) For the report may reach through the mouth of an opponent just as it reaches through the mouth of a supporter. When he hears any call whatsoever to God, and leaves off reasoning with his intellect about its soundness, though he is one of the people of inference and reflection, he has by that turned away from the call and so disbelieved. And God knows best. If it is possible that he never heard at all of any religion or call of a prophet, and never knew that there is in the world one who affirms a God (and we do not think that this occurs), then his case is subject to difference of opinion, meaning according to those who require belief by reason alone, and those who require it only with the addition of transmitted revelation. What al-Halimi said has been reported in similar terms from the Imam al-Shafi'i himself (may God be pleased with him)." al-Zarkashi said at the end of the chapter on blood-money in his commentary on the Minhaj: "al-Shafi'i has indicated the difficulty of the absence of the call (i.e., non-arrival of the call), when he said: 'I do not think anyone has not been reached by the call, except a people beyond the river, in our time.'" al-Damiri said: "al-Shafi'i said: 'No one remains who has not been reached by the call.'"

When He pointed to the punishment of those who oppose Him, He established its causes and made known that these causes are by His decree (p-391). His decree does not negate the rights of the punishment, because the matter is built on what rational people customarily understand among themselves. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿And when﴾, meaning: We send the Messengers with Our commands and Our prohibitions. And when We want to give life to a town, a good life in this world and the Hereafter, We cast into the hearts of its people the compliance with Our commands and the adherence to following Our Messengers. And when ﴿We intend﴾, and Our intention is never anything but very great, ﴿to destroy﴾, meaning: by Our greatness, ﴿a town﴾, in the future time, ﴿and We command﴾, meaning: by the greatness We have, which no one can resist disobeying, ﴿its affluent ones﴾, those who hold the command and the prohibition, ﴿to commit wickedness﴾, meaning: We lead them on gradually by granting abundant blessings and averting calamities, despite the sins they commit, and this, by being a cause of their insolence and opposition, is like commanding them to commit wickedness. ﴿So they commit wickedness therein﴾, after the Messenger had removed their excuses by conveying the message, as He said (Exalted is He): ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ [al-An'am: 44], meaning: through the tongues of the Messengers, ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and so on. ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals to scheme therein﴾ [al-An'am: 123]. He specified the affluent because others follow them, and because they are the most deserving of people to give thanks, and the most fitting to be punished when they disbelieve. It is also possible that it means: We commanded them with Our commands, so they committed wickedness in them, meaning the commands to acts of obedience, whereby it is known with certainty (p-392) that Our commands are only with these and never with other than these, because We do not command indecency. The custom has been that the affluent person is difficult to lead, and his soul hardly permits him to become a follower after having been a leader, so they disobeyed, and others followed them, because the lesser ones follow the greater ones, and they unanimously agreed upon disobedience, so We destroyed them. Ya'qub read ﴿āmarnā﴾ with a lengthened hamza, in the sense of "We multiplied," from "āmartu al-shay'" and "amartuhu fa-umir," meaning when I multiplied it. In a hadith: "The best wealth is a well-tended palm-irrigation channel and a numerous herd of mares," meaning that it is abundant in offspring. Al-Bukhari, in the chapter of tafsir, narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "In the pre-Islamic period, when a tribe increased in number, we would say: 'The Banu so-and-so have multiplied (āmara).'" The multiplication returns to the command, which is the opposite of prohibition, for it is the result of power, which is a necessary consequence of multiplicity. It is also possible that it is from al-mu'āmara (consultation), meaning: We commanded them with Our commands, but they did not comply; and they commanded Us with their commands, meaning: they asked Us for what they wanted, so We gave them that as a gradual leading on, and the attainment of their desires made them insolent, so they committed wickedness. ﴿So the word is justified﴾, meaning: it became obligatory, with no doubt as to its occurrence, ﴿against them﴾, the word with which We threatened them through the tongue of the Messenger, by the actual committing of wickedness by some of them and the silence of the rest, according to what you customarily understand among yourselves, that whoever opposes a command that is obligatory upon him deserves punishment. ﴿So We destroyed it﴾, meaning: We destroyed it with a severe destruction, suddenly, without caring for it, so We made it (p-393) like crumbled, pulverized dust. Its matter, given Our greatness, was easy; and for this reason He emphasized, saying (Exalted is He): ﴿with complete destruction﴾.
