Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 17:

When he (Allah) established that this is His way, that when He wills to destroy, He informs that He did so to those generations whom the count cannot number and the limit cannot encompass of the nations, because witnessing (i'tibar bi-l-mushahad, taking lessons from what is seen) has a greater effect on the heart and is more awe-inspiring to the soul. It is as if He said: How many times have We done that to the towns, and We did not hasten in destroying any town of them, nor did We seize them without warning; rather, We sent messengers among them and gave them respite (amlaynā lahum), until what We had known from eternity came to pass, and the appointed time that We had decreed arrived, and they reached in their sins what made them deserving of the seizing. And indeed We destroyed the people of Noah in this same manner, and they were the people of the earth, as the allusion to it has passed and the reminder of it has occurred. Their destruction was in conveying to the people of the earth what We had sent Our messengers with, of monotheism (tawhid), because that was not lightened for anyone after them. He conjoined to this implied premise His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And how many have We destroyed﴾; that is, by what We possess of greatness; and He explained the meaning of "kam" (how many) by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿of generations﴾; in this same manner.

Since the destruction by the punishment of extermination (adhab al-isti'sal) does not extend to what follows it, He introduced the preposition, so He said (Exalted is He): ﴿after Noah﴾; the one whose descendants you are, of those whom We saved (p-394) by carrying them with him; with their sins We gave them respite until We had given them an excuse, then We seized them after varying periods, so some of them were given a shorter term than others; and some of them We saved after We had surrounded them with signs of the punishment. As for those before Noah, the apparent meaning from the wording of the Torah and the silence of the Qur'an is that they were not disbelievers, and many of the exegetes stated this explicitly in the commentary on: ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213].

Since this may perhaps necessitate the question: how is the one who remains silent punished, given the possibility of his excuse by incapacity or other reasons? He said, repelling that and leaving aside the manifestation of greatness, showing gentleness toward this noble Prophet (upon him be the best of prayers and peace), in a circumstantial clause: ﴿And your Lord is sufficient﴾; that is, the One who is gracious to you by pardoning your nation and their descendants from extermination; ﴿concerning the sins of His servants﴾; that is, because He created them and decreed what is in them of all movements and stillnesses; ﴿Ever Acquainted﴾ [khabiran] from eternity; so He knows the secret and what is more hidden. As for you, you are not there; how many a person you used to see as among the great righteous, then when tested, his end revealed that he was among the most misguided of the astray; ﴿All-Seeing﴾ [basiran] of them; when they occur, nothing of them is hidden from Him. As for you, how many a person you used to see diligent in worship, yet when he is alone, he defies his Lord with grave sins.

ولَمّا تَقَرَّرَ أنَّهُ - سُبْحانَهُ - خَبِيرٌ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ

When it had been established that He, glory be to Him, is Aware of their sins;

بَعْدَ تَزْهِيدِهِ في الدُّنْيا بِما ذَكَرَ مِن مَصارِعِ الأوَّلِينَ

after His discouraging them from the worldly life by what He mentioned of the fates of the earlier peoples,

أتْبَعَهُ الإخْبارَ بِأنَّهُ يُعامِلُهم عَلى حَسَبِ عِلْمِهِ

He followed it with the information that He deals with them according to His knowledge,

عَلى وجْهٍ مُعَرِّفٍ بِعِلْمِهِ بِجَمِيعِ طَوِيّاتِهِمْ مِن خَيْرٍ وشَرٍّ

in a manner that makes known His knowledge of all their inner intentions, whether good or evil;

مُرَغِّبٍ في الآخِرَةِ مُرَهِّبٍ مِنَ الدُّنْيا

encouraging toward the Hereafter and deterring from the world;

لِأنَّها المانِعَةُ مِنَ اتِّباعِ الرُّسُلِ والتَّقَيُّدِ بِطاعَتِهِمْ

because it is the world that prevents following the messengers and being bound to obeying them,

خَوْفًا مِن نَقْصِ الحَظِّ مِنَ الدُّنْيا بِزَوالِ ما هو فِيهِ مِنَ الرِّئاسَةِ والمالِ والِانْهِماكِ في اللَّذَّةِ

out of fear of losing a share of the world through the loss of what they have of leadership, wealth, and absorption in pleasure;

جَهْلًا بِأنَّ ما قُدِّرَ لا يَكُونُ غَيْرُهُ سَواءٌ كانَ صاحِبُهُ في طاعَةٍ أوْ مَعْصِيَةٍ

out of ignorance that what has been decreed cannot be otherwise, whether its possessor is in obedience or in disobedience.

فَقالَ (تَعالى): ﴿مَن كانَ يُرِيدُ﴾

So He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever desires﴾

أيْ: إرادَةً هو فِيها في غايَةِ الإمْعانِ بِما اقْتَضاهُ طَبْعُهُ المُشارُ إلَيْهِ بِفِعْلِ الكَوْنِ

meaning: a desire in which he is at the utmost intensity, according to what his nature requires, indicated by the verb "kāna" (was/is);

ولَمّا كانَ مَدارُ مَقْصُودِ السُّورَةِ عَلى الإحْسانِ الَّذِي هو العِبادَةُ عَلى المُشاهَدَةِ

and since the central aim of the surah rests on ihsan, which is worship as if witnessing (Allah),

وكانَ ذَلِكَ مُنافِيًا لِحالِ مَن يَلْتَفِتُ إلى الدُّنْيا

and that is incompatible with the state of one who turns toward the world,

عَبَّرَ بِقَوْلِهِ (تَعالى): ﴿العاجِلَةَ﴾

He expressed it by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the hastening [world]﴾

أيْ: فَقَطْ ﴿عَجَّلْنا﴾

meaning: only; ﴿We hasten﴾

أيْ: بِعَظَمَتِنا ﴿لَهُ فِيها﴾

meaning: by Our majesty; ﴿for him therein﴾

أيْ: العاجِلَةِ ﴿ما نَشاءُ﴾

meaning: in the hastening [world]; ﴿what We will﴾

مِمّا يُرِيدُهُ لا جَمِيعَ ما يُرِيدُهُ

of what he desires, not all that he desires.

ثُمَّ أبْدَلَ مِن ”لَهُ“ قَوْلَهُ (تَعالى): ﴿لِمَن نُرِيدُ﴾

Then He substituted for "la-hu" His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for whomever We will﴾

أيْ: لا لِكُلِّ مَن أرادَ ذَلِكَ تَنْبِيهًا عَلى أنَّ ذَلِكَ بِقُوَّتِنا لا بِقُوَّةِ ذَلِكَ المُرِيدِ

meaning: not for everyone who desires that; as an alert that this is by Our power, not by the power of that desirer.

﴿ثُمَّ جَعَلْنا﴾ (p-٣٩٦) أيْ: بِما لَنا مِنَ العَظَمَةِ ﴿لَهُ﴾ أيْ: لِظاهِرِهِ وباطِنِهِ ﴿جَهَنَّمَ﴾

﴿Then We appoint﴾ (p-396) meaning: by what We have of majesty; ﴿for him﴾ meaning: for his outward and inward; ﴿Hell﴾

أيْ: الدَّرْكَةَ النّارِيَّةَ الَّتِي تَلْقى بِالتَّجَهُّمِ مَن كانَ يَلْقى الدُّنْيا وأهْلَها بِالتَّبَسُّمِ

meaning: the fiery abode, which meets with scowling those who used to meet the world and its people with smiling;

﴿يَصْلاها﴾ في الآخِرَةِ ﴿مَذْمُومًا﴾ أيْ: مَفْعُولًا بِهِ الذَّمُّ وهو ضِدُّ المَدْحِ ﴿مَدْحُورًا﴾ مَدْفُوعًا مَطْرُودًا مُبْعَدًا

﴿he will burn therein﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿blameworthy﴾ meaning: one upon whom blame is inflicted, which is the opposite of praise; ﴿rejected﴾ meaning: repelled, expelled, distanced.

فَيَنْبَغِي لِمُرِيدِ الدُّنْيا ألّا يَزالَ عَلى حَذَرٍ لِأنَّهُ لا يَنْفَكُّ مِن عَذابِ الآخِرَةِ

Therefore the one who desires the world should never cease to be on guard, for he is never free of the punishment of the Hereafter;

فَإنْ لَمْ يُعْطَ شَيْئًا مِن مُناهُ كَما أشارَ إلَيْهِ ”لِمَن نُرِيدُ“ اجْتَمَعَ لَهُ العَذابانِ كامِلَيْنِ فَقْرُ الدُّنْيا وعَذابُ الآخِرَةِ

if he is not given any of his wishes, as indicated by "for whomever We will," both punishments gather for him in full: the poverty of the world and the punishment of the Hereafter;

وإنْ أُعْطِيَ فَهو لا يُعْطى كُلَّ ما يُرِيدُ بِما أشارَ إلَيْهِ ”ما نَشاءُ“ فَيَجْتَمِعُ لَهُ عَذابُ ما مَنَعَهُ مِنها مَعَ عَذابِ الآخِرَةِ

and if he is given, he is not given all that he desires, as indicated by "what We will," so there gathers for him the punishment of what was withheld from him along with the punishment of the Hereafter.

When He mentioned the ignorant, He mentioned the knowledgeable doer who acts on his knowledge, saying (may He be exalted): ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾; that is, any desire at all, which the indefinite form indicated by "kāna" (it was) implies. ﴿And strives for it﴾; that is, he adds action to his intention, by striving. ﴿With the striving due to it﴾; that is, the striving that is proper to it, which is what it deserves of action that pleases God, in accordance with what He prescribed in His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), not any striving whatsoever, such as what the apparent sense of the Book and the Sunnah does not attest. This makes clear that intention benefits only when accompanied by action, either actually when one is able, or potentially when one is not. Then He mentioned the condition of the striving that is not accepted without it, saying (may He be exalted): ﴿while he is a believer﴾; that is, firmly established in this attribute. (p-397) As has been reported from some of the early generation (al-salaf): "Whoever does not have three things, his deed will not benefit him: a firm faith, a sincere intention, and a correct action," and he recited this verse. This firmness is the excellence (iḥsān) around which the purpose of the surah revolves. Then He ordered the reward upon it, saying: ﴿those﴾; that is, the people of high rank, for their combining the three conditions; ﴿their striving is ever thanked﴾; that is, accepted, rewarded for it with multiplication, ﴿though some of them We provide with the doors of this world, like Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and We employ them in it with what He loves; and some of them We withhold it from, as an honour to them, not as a humiliation.* So the upshot is that if worldly things are found with the saint, they do not elevate him; and if they are absent from him, they do not diminish him. Nobility and its opposite are only with God, according to deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 20:

When he had informed about his noble self concerning what points to the widening [of provision] for whomever he wills among the people of falsehood, he informed that he had decreed this in eternity, out of bounty. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿To each﴾; i.e., of the two groups: the seekers of this world and the seekers of the Hereafter, ﴿We extend﴾; i.e., with bestowal. Then He substituted from "each" the words of Him (exalted is He): ﴿these﴾; i.e., those who sought this world, We extend to them, ﴿and these﴾; those who sought the Hereafter, We extend to them, ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾; i.e., the One who is beneficent to him in all His decree. If He restricts [provision] for a believer, it is by protecting him from the transient world, which is nothing but amusement and play; and if He widens it, it is by employing it in what pleases Him and exalts His word. ﴿And the gift of your Lord is not restricted﴾; i.e., the One who originated you, the Manager of your affair, ﴿restricted﴾; i.e., prevented in this world from a believer or from a disbeliever. Rather, it fills the plain and the mountain, of gold, silver, iron, copper, jewels, fruits, the sustenance of people, of animals, and other things that none can count except Allah, to the extent that if all people gathered to collect it night and day, having no occupation other than that, it would exhaust them and they would not be able to [do so]. So glory be to the Generous, the Vast, the Giver, the Withholder.

Then He commanded consideration of this giving, in a manner that encourages toward the Hereafter and makes one abstain from this world. So He (Exalted) said, commanding reflection: ﴿Look﴾. And He showed that their condition, because of its strangeness, is worthy of being asked about; so He (Exalted) said: ﴿how We have favoured﴾; that is, by what We possess of overpowering greatness; ﴿some of them over others﴾; in this worldly life, through provision. Thus the superior comes to employ the inferior, and the inferior is eager to serve the one favoured and takes pride in drawing near to him; even though God's provision, which is His giving, is equal in relation to all; He created what exists in this world for the righteous and the wicked alike, and all are eager to take from the provisions more than their sufficiency, which are more than them. This differentiation was nothing but by the compulsion of a Powerful One who subdued them to it, and He is the One who is exempt from deficiency and has attained (p-399) every perfection; so He deserves that the desire of the one who desires be directed to none but Him.

When He alerted that what we see of differentiation is purely by His power, He informed that everything after death is likewise, without any difference; so He said: ﴿And the Hereafter﴾; He emphasized the report about what is in it, which necessarily entails emphasizing the information about its existence, because of their denial of it; ﴿is greater in degrees﴾; than this worldly life; ﴿and greater in preference﴾; first in regard to Paradise and Hellfire themselves, and second in regard to the degrees in Paradise and the levels in Hellfire. Since knowledge here is restricted to sins, it is mentioned after the preference in this world; and perhaps in that there is an indication that most of those who are increased in this world will have their increase become a deficiency in their Hereafter, because of a sin they committed or a shortcoming they committed. And since knowledge in what follows, in His saying (Exalted): ﴿And your Lord knows best﴾ [al-Isra': 55], is absolute, He left aside the vices after it and joined to that left-aside matter the virtues; so He (Exalted) said: ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra': 55]; etc.; so whoever has a noble soul and a lofty aspiration, it is incumbent upon him to abstain from a perishing loftiness for the sake of the enduring loftiness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 22:

When it had been established by what came before that to Him, glory be to Him, belongs all command, and that He is characterized by all perfection, exalted above any blemish of deficiency, He produced the conclusion that there is no god besides Him. So He said, (exalted is He) — addressing the head (of the community), because that has greater effect on the souls of the followers; and as an indication that no one else monotheizes Him in the true sense of monotheism — and it is permissible that it be a general address to everyone who may be addressed with it: ﴿Do not set up with Allah﴾, who possesses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿another god﴾. The secret of His saying ﴿another﴾ will come shortly: that it is understood from the concomitance (of the two). ﴿So you will sit﴾, i.e., so that there will result from that that you sit, i.e., you become (one) in this world, before the Hereafter, ﴿reproached﴾. And since reproach may be borne by some people along with the attainment of their hope, He made clear that (the reproach comes) along with failure, so He said (exalted is He): ﴿forsaken﴾, i.e., not granted victory in what you intend, without anyone being able to avail you with an intercession or otherwise.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 23:

When this prohibition that makes His tawhid binding struck the ears, He followed it with a declaration of the command to that effect. In doing so, He combined both the explicit command and the explicit prohibition, in the form of a statement, after declaring Him free of any partner, by singling Him out for worship. This was to inform of the greatness of the station. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾, meaning: He forbade you from that and commanded it. ﴿Your Lord﴾, meaning: the One who is good to you, decreed a binding command, definitively settled, already determined, which admits of no dispute. Then He explained this command by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you worship not except Him﴾, meaning: you and all the people of your call, who are all of creation. ﴿Except Him﴾, for that is the true goodness.

When He commanded the recognition of the right of the absolutely Good One, drawing attention to the obligation of that through the name "the Lord," He followed it with the command to recognize the right of the first of those who nurture creation, saying: (p-401) ﴿And to the two parents﴾, meaning: and do good, that is, direct goodness toward them both; ﴿good treatment﴾, by following the truth if they are both ḥanīfs (upright monotheists), thankful for His blessings, like Abraham and Noah, peace be upon them both, for that increases their good deeds; and by disavowing them in falsehood, for that lightens their burden of sin; and by gentleness toward them, so long as it does not lead to corruption; ﴿so that Allah may be with you﴾, for He is with those who are God-fearing and those who are doers of good.

Since He, glorified is He, knows what is in human nature of weariness with parents when they reach old age, He said: ﴿If﴾, emphasized by adding "mā" to the conditional particle, for greater affirmation of the meaning, out of concern for the matter of the two parents; ﴿they reach old age with you﴾, meaning: they become dependent upon you, so that they have no guardian other than you; ﴿old age﴾. He negated every possibility that the one seeking to find fault might cling to by His saying: ﴿either or both of them﴾, so that they become weak, such that they are in your care. ﴿Then do not say to them "uff"﴾, meaning: do not show irritation toward them. The surah of al-Aḥqāf contains much that is beneficial here. Then He explicitly stated what the speech forbids by way of a stronger inference (min bāb al-awlā), magnifying the station, saying: ﴿And do not scold them﴾ for what you do not like. "Nahr" is rebuke with harshness and shouting.

The Ustādh Abu al-Ḥasan al-Ḥarrālī, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book on the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh, the foundations of Islamic legal theory): The usūliyyūn (scholars of legal theory) have been excessively inclined to cite, within this category (that is, the category of inferring the implied from the implicating, and the lesser from the greater), His saying: ﴿Do not say to them "uff"﴾, on the basis that "uff" is in their view the least thing by which a father is disobeyed. That deviates from the patterns of eloquence and the wisdom of the matter, for there is nothing more severe in disobedience than "uff," since it is said only of what is loathsome and despicable. For this reason He conjoined to it: ﴿And do not scold them﴾, because it does not necessarily follow from it that it is equal or greater. It is not appropriate, in what is the lesser, to conjoin to it something that necessarily entails equality or greater, just as if someone said: "Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does a qīrāṭ will see it," it would not be appropriate to conjoin the second to the first, since the first already implies it. Perhaps that is a slip, and someone may have erred in it, yet it was followed in its wake without regard to his statement. End of quotation.

When He forbade disobedience toward them, giving precedence to averting harm, He commanded kindness toward them, to secure benefit, saying: ﴿And speak to them﴾, meaning: instead of scolding and other things, ﴿a generous word﴾, meaning: good and beautiful, which Allah and His Messenger are pleased with, along with what appears in it of gentleness, tenderness, compassion, consoling the heart, and easing the soul, as good manners and beautiful chivalry require. (p-403) Among that is that you do not address them by their names, but rather with "O my father" and "O my mother," and the like.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 24:

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾. Since the bird lowers its wing when it is humbled, He used this image for his tenderness toward them, out of regard for their rights: the words of the Exalted, ﴿the wing of humility﴾, meaning the wing of your humility. He clarified the intended sense by the words of the Exalted, ﴿out of mercy﴾, meaning not merely for the sake of obeying the command or fear of shame, but out of mercy toward them. This means you should never cease reminding yourself of the commands and prohibitions, and of the kindness they showed you before, so that they become in need of you, when in fact you were the person in greatest need of them. This should become a constant disposition in you, for the soul indeed commands to evil, unless it is led toward good through various kinds of encouragement and warning, and through deep reflection on the realities of affairs and the wonders of what is decreed.

For this reason He followed it with His words, the Exalted, commanding that one should not suffice with one's mercy, which has no permanence, for that does not repay their right, but rather should seek for them enduring mercy. ﴿And say: My Lord﴾, meaning, O You who showed kindness to me by their tenderness toward me, until they raised me and put me before themselves, ﴿have mercy on them﴾ with Your generosity, with Your enduring mercy and Your bounty, ﴿as they raised me﴾ with their mercy toward me, ﴿when I was small﴾. And this is specific to the Muslims, by the verse ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and it is not abrogated (naskh, abrogation).

He, glory be to Him, was most eloquent in enjoining them, for He began by pairing kindness to them with His own Oneness, placed it in the same thread, and concluded with supplication for their salvation, as a reward for their deeds and in gratitude to them. He also tightened the matter of caring for them, so much so that He did not grant license in even the slightest degradation of them, despite the things that provoke impatience, and despite circumstances into which patience can hardly enter within the limit of capacity, except through great training.

[p. 404]

Since this matter is extremely difficult, he warns against neglecting it, by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Your Lord﴾; that is, the One who truly does good to you; for it is He who inclined toward you those who raise you, and He who helped you to do so. ﴿Knows best﴾; that is, better than you do; ﴿what is in your souls﴾; of intending righteousness toward them both and otherwise. So let none of you show other than what he conceals, for that will not benefit him nor save him, unless he compels his soul to that which will be a cause of their mercy toward him. ﴿If you are﴾; that is, in a state that is innate in you; ﴿righteous﴾; that is, God-fearing; or doing good in reality. Righteousness (ṣalāḥ) is the soundness of action in accordance with what the evidence calls for. He indicates that this is not attained except by disciplining the soul and making it return again and again after each lapse, by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾; that is, those who return (al-awwābīn) to good, time after time, after their souls have bolted away from it; ﴿Forgiving﴾; that is, of complete concealment; as an admonition to whoever has fallen short and then returned from it, on the basis that he is forgiven.

When he had urged kindness to the two parents in particular, he generalized the command to it for every kinsman and others, saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾, on the side of the father or the mother, even if distant; "his right" (haqqahu wa) "give" (ātin), "the needy" (al-miskīn), even if he is not a relative; ﴿and the wayfarer﴾, who is the traveler cut off from his wealth, so that you may be pious and doing good.

When he encouraged spending, and the self's action is rarely balanced between excess and deficiency, he followed that with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And do not squander﴾, by scattering wealth extravagantly (isrāf), which is spending it on what is not fitting. In His saying ﴿squandering (tabdhīr)﴾ there is an alert that ascending toward the courtyard of squandering is better than descending into the narrow pass of stinginess and niggardliness. "Tabdhīr" (squandering): spreading the hand over wealth according to desire, recklessly. As for generosity, it is by a known measure, because it is following God's command regarding financial rights; some of them are known by quantity, and some are known by quality, such as supporting the people of the faith and thanking those who have done good to you, and the like. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about squandering and said: spending wealth in other than its right. And from Mujahid (may Allah be pleased with him): If a person spent all his wealth in what is right, it would not be squandering; but if he spent a mudd in falsehood, it would be squandering.

Then he gave the reason for that in His saying: (p-406) ﴿Indeed, the squanderers﴾; that is, by natural disposition and inherent nature; ﴿were﴾; that is, in a state of being firmly rooted in it; ﴿brothers of the devils﴾; that is, all of them; those far removed from mercy, those burning in the curse; for their action is the action of fire, which is the greater part of their constituents; and it is the burning of whatever it reaches, whether for benefit or for no benefit. So when they find nothing, they take what is not theirs. The Arabs say of every one who keeps close to the custom of a people and follows their affair: "He is their brother."

And since moderation is more conducive to gratitude, and squandering is more leading to disbelief, He (Exalted) said: ﴿And the Satan was﴾; that is, this kind, far removed from every good, burning with every evil; ﴿to his Lord﴾; that is, the One who did good to him by bringing him into existence and nurturing him; ﴿ungrateful﴾; that is, one who conceals what he is able to conceal of His manifest signs and His dazzling blessings, along with the proof.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 28:

When He had commanded what is preferable in the state of having (wealth), He commanded the like of it in the state of lacking; so He said, emphasizing it, as an alert that turning away from them should be considered something far-fetched and reprehensible: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾; that is, from all those mentioned before, those to whom you were commanded to give, due to a matter that compelled you to that, which you could not avoid, because you do not find anything to give them; so you turned away out of modesty, not out of intent to refuse; rather ﴿seeking﴾; that is, desiring ﴿mercy﴾; that is, honor and abundance; ﴿from your Lord﴾, the Abundant in Goodness; ﴿which you hope for﴾. So when it comes to you, share it with them. ﴿Then speak to them﴾, in the state of turning away, ﴿a gentle word﴾; that is, one full of ease, which opens their hearts and expands their hope, because that is closer to the way of the God-fearing, the good-doers, those with whom I am (p-407). Abu Hayyan said: It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, had nothing to give after the revelation of this verse, and he was asked, he would say: "May Allah grant us and you from His bounty." End of quote.

Here he has placed "seeking" in the position of "poverty," because it is its cause; so he has placed the effect in the position of the cause.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 29:

When He commanded generosity, which is the necessary consequence of nobility (karam), He forbade stinginess (bukhl), which is the necessary consequence of blameworthiness (lawm), in a context that repels from it and from extravagance (israf). So He said, giving an example and beginning with the example of niggardliness: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, through stinginess; ﴿meaning, as if it were shackled with a collar by withholding﴾; ﴿so that you cannot extend it﴾; ﴿and do not spread it out completely﴾, through giving; ﴿so that you sit down﴾, meaning you come to be like one who is seated, by grasping; ﴿blameworthy﴾, meaning deeply entrenched in that for which you are blamed in the sight of God, because that is among what He has forbidden; and in the sight of people; ﴿and by spreading out﴾ [in lavish giving]; ﴿depleted﴾, meaning cut off from you because what you rely on has departed and withdrawn from you; and each of the two states exceeds the limit of moderation.

Since the cause of stinginess is fear of poverty, and the cause of expansiveness is love of enriching the giver, he said, consoling His Messenger (ﷺ) for what used to burden him of excessive concern about widening provision for those who asked him, that this is only for the training of the servants with what sets them right, not for humiliation of the one whose provision is restricted, nor for honoring the one whose provision is expanded: ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾; (p-408); i.e., the one who is good to you; ﴿extends provision to whom He wills﴾; extending it to him, not to others; ﴿and restricts [it]﴾; i.e., He likewise constricts; whether He withholds His hand or extends it; ﴿And if Allah had extended provision to His servants, they would have transgressed upon the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 27]; but He (exalted be He) does not carry the one to whom He extends [provision] to the full extent of his desire, nor does He bring the one from whom He withholds [provision] to the utmost of what he dislikes. So follow His practice of moderation in your spending upon His servants; ﴿Indeed, He is ever⁠﴾; i.e., a being who is in the utmost capability; ﴿of His servants, Acquainted⁠﴾; i.e., reaching the utmost in knowledge; ﴿Seeing⁠﴾; i.e., reaching the utmost in sight regarding all of the withholding and extending for them, [whether it is] a benefit or a harm.

When Allah, glorified is He, had completed what He willed of the commandment concerning the fundamentals, and what follows from it, and concluded it with what He had established, namely that the grasping and the extending of provision are from Him, and no stratagem avails in that, He enjoined them concerning the subsidiary matters, because they were in the utmost weakness. They used to kill their daughters for fear of poverty, and the very name "daughter" had become, through long-standing abhorrence of it among them, a cause of harshness. So in forbidding that, He addressed them directly, to make known how far removed he (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) was from this practice, both before Islam and after it, saying: ﴿And do not kill your children﴾, expressing it with the word "child," which calls for tenderness and compassion, ﴿for fear of poverty﴾, that is, a poverty that is anticipated and has not yet occurred. Then He joined to that, as a resumed statement, His saying: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾, placing the pronoun referring to the children first, because poverty is something expected to result from spending on them, and not yet present at the time of killing. This differs from the verse in "Al-An'am," for its context indicates that poverty is present at the time of killing, and killing is for inability to spend. Then He gave as the reason something more general than that, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, their killing﴾, that is, absolutely, whether for this reason or another, ﴿is a great sin (khit'an kabiran)﴾, that is, a sin, ﴿great.﴾ Al-Rummani said: "al-khit'" (with a kasra, then a sukun) is only committed deliberately, in opposition to what is right, whereas "al-khata'" (with a fatha) may occur without deliberate intent.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 32:

Since the killing of children involves a share of stinginess (bukhl), and the act of fornication (zina) involves a motive toward excess (israf), He followed it with it, saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾; that is, do not draw near to it in the slightest degree, by doing anything of its preliminaries, even by letting a passing thought of it occur to the mind; ﴿fornication﴾. Although the most common cause of its commission by women is need and the seeking of increase; and in it there is a meaning of killing the child by wasting its lineage; and in it there is a causing of a soul to come into being in falsehood, just as killing causes its annihilation in falsehood. He expressed it by "approaching" to magnify it, because of the corrupt consequences it leads to, which lead to strife, including killing and other things. Then he gave the reason for it with his saying, emphasizing it, to convey the strength of the warning against it, because of the intensity of the soul's inclination toward it: ﴿Indeed, it was an indecency﴾; that is, a state that is never separated from it; ﴿and an evil﴾; that is, excessively ugly; and He had forbidden you from indecency in the verse of justice and beneficence; ﴿and evil is the way﴾; that is, how evil a path it is! (p-410) Expressing it as a "way" indicates the multitude of those who engage in it, by pointing to the breadth of its course.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 33:

When he (Allah) had completed the prohibition against these two matters, which are united in describing indecency and in their cause, namely the killing of a child by slaying and what is in its meaning, He followed them with the general prohibition of killing, which among its causes is the acquisition of wealth. So He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And do not kill the soul﴾; that is, on account of the preciousness which its Creator has placed in it; ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾; that is, the Supreme King, to whom all command belongs; by Islam, or by covenant; ﴿except by right﴾; that is, by a matter by which Allah makes lawful that sanctity which was [previously] in place. Thus the causes forbidden become, through the prohibition of their effects: withholding what exists out of stinginess, then squandering it extravagantly, then acquiring what is lost through transgression. Then He joined to it what the context indicates as its implied supposition, which is: "Whoever kills a soul without right has disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." ﴿And whoever is killed﴾; that is, whose killing occurs at the hand of any killer whatsoever; ﴿wrongfully﴾; that is, by whatever injustice it may be, without his having committed one of three things: disbelief, adultery after being married, and killing a believer intentionally and aggressively; ﴿We have certainly given﴾; that is, by the greatness We possess; ﴿to his heir﴾; that is, whether he is a relative or a ruler; ﴿authority﴾; that is, a commanding power; ﴿so let him not commit excess﴾ the heir; or: so do not commit excess, O heir; ﴿in killing﴾, by killing other than the killer, and let him not exceed his right in any way; ﴿indeed he﴾; that is, the slain; ﴿was supported﴾ (p-411) in this world, by what Allah has instilled in natures of the indecency of killing, and everyone's aversion to it, and the hatred of the killer, and the revulsion from him, and the restraining of his hand; and in the Hereafter, by taking his right from him without injustice or heedlessness. Whoever is confident of this abandons excess, for it is either out of fear of loss, or to instill fear of recurrence.

When He forbade raiding lives and the women (al-abda') that are their cause, He followed it with the prohibition of plundering what is their equivalent, because by it their subsistence is sustained, namely wealth. He began with the most deserving of this prohibition, because of the intensity of greed for it, owing to the weakness of its owner. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not approach﴾, that is, let alone eat, ﴿the property of the orphan﴾. He expressed it with "approaching," which comes before taking, as a magnification of the station. ﴿Except in the way that is best﴾, from among the ways of approaching it, which is to manage it with what is beneficial, in order to grow the orphan's wealth. ﴿Until he reaches﴾ the orphan ﴿his maturity (ashuddah)﴾, which is the perceiving of rushd (sound judgment) in him after his reaching puberty.

When the bequest (wasiyyah) was a kind of covenant ('ahd), He commanded the fulfilment of what is more general than it. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fulfil﴾, that is, carry out this kind in its time and place and in all that the matter covenanted depends upon and is connected with, ﴿the covenant﴾ (p-412), that is, by means of it, so that the fulfilment of it is realized and no deficiency occurs in it. It is the contract that is made to secure trust.

When knowledge of breaking and of fulfilment was certain, the covenant itself was as if it were the one questioned about that, and so it would be a watcher over the one who does it. So He, exalted is He, said, warning against violation: ﴿Indeed the covenant was﴾, that is, a firmly established state concerning it, ﴿questioned﴾, that is, about every one who made a covenant: did he fulfil it? Or it is questioned about by everyone from whom questioning is possible.

When the estimation by measure or weight was among the hidden trusts, like managing an orphan's property, and entrusting it was like a matter already agreed upon, He followed it with His saying: ﴿Give full measure when you measure﴾. That is, [He commanded] the measuring itself, because it is a perceptible matter in which there is no confusion or ambiguity. Since it applies both to the one who gives and the one who receives, He said: ﴿when you measure﴾, that is, for others. If you measure for yourselves, then there is no blame on you if you take less than your right and do not give full measure. ﴿And weigh﴾, that is, weigh while ﴿with the qistas﴾ (the balance, a scale of justice), that is, the scale of justice, which is the most upright of scales. He increased the emphasis of its meaning by saying, may He be exalted: ﴿the straight﴾, without any unfairness, as was stated regarding measuring, in the same manner. ﴿That﴾ (p-413), that is, this lofty matter which We have commanded you to do, ﴿is better﴾ for you in this world and the Hereafter, even if it appears to you that something else is better, ﴿and better in outcome﴾, that is, better in its consequence in both abodes. The word ta'wil (outcome, interpretation) is a form of "taf'il" derived from awwal (return), meaning the return to its origin. The elative form (af'al al-tafdil) here is used for the sake of fairness and to give latitude, that is, on the assumption that there is good in each of the two options, this which we have mentioned is greater in good. A sensible person should not be content to settle for less for himself.

Since that is something the hearts testify to as good, and its opposites are something the souls recognize as ugly, because Allah (Exalted) created man disposed to that, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Righteousness is that to which the heart is at rest and the soul is reassured; sin is that which stirs in the heart and wavers in the breast, even if the muftis issue you fatwas [permitting it] and they give you fatwas." And he said: "Among what people have obtained from the words of the first prophethood is: if you feel no shame, then do as you will." Having gathered the pronouns, glorified is He, He followed this with what includes both them and others, so He said (Exalted) — making the pronoun singular so that the prohibition is directed equally at each one of the plural, and at the singular, both in the state of togetherness and in the state of being alone —: ﴿And do not﴾; that is: do what you have been commanded of that, and refrain from what you have been forbidden of it, because of the necessary knowledge established in natural dispositions of its goodness and beauty. And do not ﴿follow﴾; that is: O human, do not pursue, striving, by tracing traces, ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾; of that and other things, each thing according to its measure; especially slander and false accusation. For whatever matter requires certainty, one is not content with less than that in it, and whatever is satisfied with conjecture, one stops at it. Then he gave the reason for that, warning, by saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight﴾, which are the two paths of perception; ﴿and the heart﴾, which is the instrument of perception. Then he magnified the matter by saying (Exalted): ﴿all of those﴾; that is, these great things, high in benefit, wondrous in their creation; and "ulā'ika" and all demonstrative names are used to refer to the rational and to others, as in his saying:

*He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days.*

﴿will be﴾; that is, by a promise that does not fail; ﴿about it﴾; that is, about it alone; ﴿questioned﴾; by a questioning specific to it: whether its possessor employed it in seeking knowledge, striving in that, so that upon reaching the realities he would act in what pleases Allah and avoid what angers Him, or not? The first movement of the soul is "al-sābiḥ" (the passing thought), then "al-khātir" (the fleeting notion), then "al-irāda" (the intention) and "al-'azīma" (the resolve). One is held accountable for the intention and the resolve, because they fall under choice, so obligation attaches to them. As for the first two, which do not fall under choice, He lightened this for us by not holding us accountable for them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 37:

Since pride and haughtiness are the greatest barrier to knowledge, which calls to every good, and a sickness with the sickness of ignorance, which carries one to every evil, He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And do not walk﴾; that is, any kind of walking; and He confirmed the meaning with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿upon the earth﴾; that is, its kind; ﴿exultantly﴾; which is intense joy that is accompanied by conceit; because that is among the follies of the soul, driven by the recklessness of desire and the call of lust, and by the deficiencies it has been created with. For it is not becoming except after attaining all the hopes that are pursued with earnestness, and that will never be the case for any created being. Therefore He gave the reason for it with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed you will not tear through﴾; that is, not even by the least of means; ﴿the earth﴾; that is, you will not cut it by traveling from your place to its far edge; ﴿and you will never reach﴾; that is, in any way at all; ﴿the mountains in height﴾; that is, the height of all the mountains, by walking over them. So if you are unable, with your power and knowledge, to draw a straight line across the breadth of the earth (p-416) despite earnest effort and striving, and to reach its pegs by stretching upward, then what do you boast of, and by what do you show pride, so as to strut about? And that is the act of one who has attained all that he hoped for.

Then he magnified all that has preceded of the forbidden acts and of the opposites of the commanded acts, by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿All that﴾; that is, the matter far removed from noble conduct; ﴿was﴾; that is, a state not separated from it; and since the evil deed (sayyi'ah) has come to have the status of nouns, like "ithm" (sin) and "dhamb" (offense), and the status of adjectives has departed from it, He construed it as masculine and described it with that, so He said (exalted is He): ﴿its evil﴾; and He increased its ugliness by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿in the sight of your Lord﴾; that is, the One who bestows upon you a bounty that deserves no response except gratitude; ﴿disliked﴾; that is, He treats it with the treatment accorded to what is disliked, by forbidding it, condemning its doer, and punishing him. A person of intellect does not do what displeases one who has bestowed favor upon him, out of shame before him; and if not, then out of fear of the cutting off of his bounty, and submission to the might of his dominion. It is also possible that the intended meaning of this singular form is the Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), as an indication that no one other than him can fully comply with this meaning as it should be, because no one knows knowledge in the way that he possesses it, equally; and because when the head is addressed with something, the followers are most receptive to it; and it is with this that I am concerned.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 39:

When these commands and prohibitions were completed in this most judicious manner and most upright order, He pointed to their great station and firm perfection by His saying, by way of resumption (istinaf), alerting the listener so that he would ask about it: ﴿That is﴾; that is, the matter that is very exalted; ﴿of what your Lord has revealed﴾; that is, sent down secretly; ﴿to you﴾; ﴿of wisdom﴾, which cannot be annulled nor can anything like it be brought; namely, calling to good and forbidding evil. Among the wisdom of these matters mentioned, from the commands and prohibitions, is that they did not admit abrogation (naskh) in any of the sacred laws; rather they were thus in every religious community.

When He had made clear that ignorance is the cause of every evil, and shirk was the greatest ignorance, He followed it, so that the prohibition against it would be at the beginning and at the end, as a sign of its extreme ugliness, joining it (ʿatfan) to the prohibitions that preceded, with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And do not make﴾; or there is understood for it what it is joined to, such as: so adhere to it; and do not make ﴿with Allah﴾; that is, the Greatest King, to whom belongs all command; ﴿another god﴾.

Since they, out of their obstinacy, would sometimes make the enumeration of the names into an enumeration of the named entities, as is reported in the occasion of revelation of ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Isra: 110], He (Exalted) said, while conveying the sense of association with otherness: ﴿another﴾; for that is the greatest ignorance, which He forbade (p-418) following; ﴿lest you be cast﴾; that is, so that you will be dealt with in the Hereafter in confinement; ﴿into Hell﴾; with the rapidity of it and the inability to remedy, like the treatment of one who is thrown down from a height; while you are ﴿blameworthy﴾; that is, censured for what you did after being reproached; ﴿rejected﴾; that is, cast out after abandonment. These two attributes are more hideous than the two attributes of reproach and abandonment in the first verse, as is His custom (Exalted) to begin with the lighter, to lead His servants gradually. Shirk was the most ignorant of ignorance because it is evident that a god can only be one in essence, so it does not divide; and in attribute, so it has no like. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that these eighteen verses were on the tablets of Musa (peace be upon him); the first of them being: ﴿Do not make with Allah another god﴾ [al-Isra: 22]; and they are ten verses in the Torah, whose opening and closing were made the prohibition of shirk, because tawhid is the head of every wisdom and its cornerstone; and whoever lacks it, his wisdom and his knowledge do not benefit him, even if he surpasses the sages in them and his head reaches the heavens. The books of philosophy did not suffice against them, and they are more astray from the religion of Allah than cattle.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 40:

Since their claim that the angels are God's daughters was a claim based on a real connection, because He has something similar to them in the most specific attribute, which is divinity, and since their worship of the angels was a confirmation of that claim, and this was more than mere polytheism out of ignorance, He pursued it in the manner of rebuke and reproach, as a warning about the evidence of its corruption. It is connected to what preceded of the prohibition of polytheism (p-419) by the conjunction with the fa' of causation (fa' al-sabab) after "ma" (what), following the resumption (al-istie'naf) with the hamzah of denial. So it is as if it had been said: "Do not do that as these people did, who went to excess in ignorance. They attributed to Him, from among His creation, the lesser of the two parts, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Nahl in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And they assign to God daughters﴾ [al-Nahl 16:57]. Then they worshipped that part, although they do not accept it for themselves." Then He turned to them, addressing them in a way that indicates the extremity of anger, and said: ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons﴾, meaning: has the One who has been good to you created sons and daughters, so that He favoured you with good to you, while you deny Him? ﴿With sons﴾, who are the better of the two kinds of offspring. "And" (He did not do good to Himself by sharing sons with you). Rather, "He has taken" (ittakhadha), expressed with the form of iftiʿal (the reflexive form), because whoever turns to one of the two kinds, while able to have the other, is only one who has an intense desire for what he turned to. ﴿From among the angels﴾, who are the closest of His servants, as offspring. Then the loss of the state of being a child and the handling of its causes were not enough for them, until they made what He took ﴿females﴾. So He is content for Himself, and He is your God, the Creator, the Provider, with what you would not be content with for yourselves. You have reached, in your dislike of it in some states, the point of killing [daughters]. So He became a partner with you in daughters, while He specifies for you, to the exclusion of Himself, the sons? That is contrary (p-420) to your custom, for slaves are not given the best, and the lesser belongs to the masters. He first expressed it as "sons" rather than "males" because the term "son" is more pleasing to the ear and satisfies the one who is given the good news of it, without consideration of the outcome, and it may be a term for the feminine of the verbs. Also, the term "male" has a shared meaning. In the second part He expressed it with "females" to convey softness through the meaning of the word. Also, they are daughters by equivalence. It is possible that the verse be understood through ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each part omits what is mentioned in the other), so the sense would be: "with sons, and He is content for Himself with daughters; and He singled you out in your kind, which is the weakest of kinds, with males; and He took from among the angels, some of whom are able to lift the earth and turn its bottom upward, females, which are of utmost softness." For this reason He resumed the denial against them, magnifying it with His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed you are saying﴾, and emphasized it, because of their laxity regarding Him and their audacity toward Him, with His saying (exalted is He): ﴿a word﴾, and He increased this with His saying: ﴿momentous﴾, meaning: in ignorance and fabrication against Him and against His angels, who do not disobey Him in what He commands them and who do what they are commanded. Yet you attribute offspring to Him, and offspring are among the characteristics of bodies. Then you prefer yourselves over Him (p-421), so you assign to Him what you dislike.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 41:

When there is in this such clarity that it is not hidden from humankind, and they did not return, He indicated that they have similar aversion to similar clarity. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified⁠﴾; that is, We directed (ṭarraqnā) a great direction with kinds of the methods of clarity: from lessons (ʿibar), wisdom (ḥikam), parables (amthāl), rulings (aḥkām), proofs (ḥujaj), and signs (aʿlām), in the molds of promise (waʿd), threat (waʿīd), command (amr), and prohibition (nahy), the clear (muḥkam) and the ambiguous (mutashābih), and other than that; ﴿in this Qur'an⁠﴾ through these methods, that which has no dust upon it; and We varied it from one aspect to another and from one example to another. And "taṣrīf" (diversification) linguistically means turning a thing from one direction to another; then it became a metaphor for clarification (tabyīn), as stated by Abū Ḥayyān.

Since that is established in natures, and in minds there are likenesses whose brides emerge from their canopies with the slightest turn of the soul, the admonition with them was named reminder (tadhkīr), by what is known; so He (Exalted) said: ﴿That they may take heed⁠﴾ (liyadhdhakkarū); that is, a type of reminder, by what the assimilation (idghām) points to; for He - glorified be He - is Generous, and is pleased with little. This is in the recitation of the majority; and Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī recited it with the dhāl sukūn and the kāf ḍammah, indicating that nothing of all that is in the Qur'an comes out of the intellect; rather it is established in natures, and it has witnesses in the souls and the horizons, which a person summons with the slightest hint and the easiest alert, when what veils them from the intellect of desires (ḥuẓūẓ) and preoccupations (shawāghil) is removed. (p-422) And He (Exalted) followed it with His saying, wondering at them: ﴿But it increases them not⁠﴾ — the diversification — ﴿except in aversion⁠﴾ from hearing, let alone remembrance; because they believe that this is not proofs; rather it is a fallacy and a deception aimed at turning them away from what they are upon, which they became accustomed to and received from their fathers, and the ages have prolonged in them the belief that it is true.

Then it was as if it were said: "What will He do to them?" So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿Say﴾ (to them), and do not despair of the return of some of them: ﴿If there were with Him other gods, as they say﴾ — that is, your Lord, whose attributes of beneficence and transcendence have already been mentioned — from these statements which, if the greatest of you were to say them about the least of you while meaning their reality, he would become a laughingstock for the servants. ﴿Then they would have sought﴾ — that is, they would have sought earnestly — ﴿a path to the Lord of the Throne﴾ — that is, the Possessor of the greatest, encompassing throne, whoever attains Him being singular in the management (of affairs) — ﴿a way﴾ — that is, a traversable road by which they might reach Him, in order to overpower Him and remove His dominion, as you see the kings of the world doing with one another; or in order to gain a favor with Him that would bring them near to Him. He stated "the Throne" explicitly to depict His greatness and to specify the object of the seeking, and the object sought.

Then He declared Himself exalted above that, out of glorification, and above every deficiency. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿Glory be to Him﴾; that is, He is utterly removed from every trace of deficiency. ﴿And exalted is He﴾; that is, He rose to the greatest height (p-423) of loftiness through attributes of perfection. ﴿Far above what they say﴾; of these deficiencies, which none of the sensible among His creatures would accept for himself, let alone one of your chiefs. How then of the Most High, the Exalted?! He used the verbal noun in its bare form in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿highly exalted﴾, to indicate that the act is in reality unadorned, even though it came in the pattern of reciprocity (taf'ul), to indicate intensification. ﴿Great﴾; your minds cannot bear to stand upon its reality, nor do you grasp of Him more than the meaning of this description as you understand it, according to what you customarily conventionalise:

*The matter is greater than the saying of any speaker,*
*whether the eloquent make it delicate or make it grand.*

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 44:

Then he (the author) began again to explain the greatness of this declaration of God's transcendence, joined with the attribute of perfection. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿Glorify﴾; that is, they produce the greatest declaration of transcendence (tasbih); ﴿Him﴾; that is, the Greatest God, whose attributes of majesty and honour have already been mentioned specifically; ﴿the seven heavens﴾; all of them; ﴿and the earth﴾; likewise; ﴿and whoever is in them﴾; of those possessed of intellect; ﴿and there is not a thing﴾; that is, "and not" (wa-ma); and he intensified the negation, so He (Exalted) said: ﴿of anything﴾; that is, of anything endowed with intellect or otherwise; ﴿but glorifies﴾; that is, declares Him transcendent; ﴿[Him] with His praise﴾; that is, by describing Him with what belongs to Him of the attributes of perfection, by the signs of Him (Exalted) in that thing which point to both negation and affirmation. This glorification is by the tongue of speech from whoever is capable of it, and by the tongue of state from it and from others, "as the wall said to the peg: Why are you piercing me? He said: Ask him who is hammering me." It is glorification from many directions, so that those who know may hear it with the hearing of understanding and clarity of mind: from the aspect of its own essence in its creation; then in the meaning of its attribute, by its need, in terms of its origination, of a Maker who brought it into existence, eternal and not made; and from the aspect of its perfection, to His being a Governor and Wise; and from the aspect of its perishing, to His being—despite that—Capable, Choosing, Dominant, Compelling... and so on. This is unlike what would be the case if glorification were restricted to the tongue of speech, for then it would be of a single kind. He further guided to this by His words (Exalted): ﴿but you do not understand﴾; rather than "you do not hear"; ﴿their glorification﴾; because of your turning away from reflection and your aversion to hearing the Reminder, which is the greatest of its means. This applies to the common people; as for the elect, they hear the glorification of inanimate things. Al-Bukhari related from ʿAbd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "We used to count the signs as a blessing, while you count them as a warning. We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey when the water ran short. He said: 'Seek some remaining water.' They brought a vessel containing a little water, and he put his hand into the vessel and said: 'Come to the blessed purifying water, and the blessing is from Allah.' Indeed I saw the water gushing from between the fingers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was honoured, exalted, revered, and magnified, forever and ever; and we used to hear the glorification of food while it was being eaten." The glorification of pebbles is well known. In the Psalms of David (peace be upon him) there is much repetition of this verse and an exhortation to reflect upon it. In Psalm 68 it says: "Let the heavens praise him, the earth, the seas, and everything that moves in them." In Psalm 85: "There is none like you, O my Lord and my God, nor like your works, for all the nations you have made shall come and bow down before you, O Lord, and they shall glorify your name, for you are great and you work wonders." In Psalm 88: "With your mighty arm you scattered your enemies. The heavens are yours, the earth is yours; you founded the world with all that is in it; you created the north and the south; Tabor and Hermon sing praises to your name. Yours is strength and dominion; your hand is strong and your right hand is exalted. With justice and judgement you established your throne; mercy and truth go before your face. Blessed is the people who know your praise." In Psalm 95: "Sing to the Lord a new song; all the earth sings to the Lord; bow down to the Lord in the splendour of his holiness, for all the earth trembles before him; say among the nations: the Lord is King; he has established the world so that it shall not be moved; he judges the peoples with equity; let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad; let the sea roar and its fullness; let the field exult and all that is in it; then all the trees of the wood shall sing before the Lord." In Psalm 97: "To God all the earth sings; shout, and rejoice, and sing praises to the Lord." In Psalm 148: "Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him from the heights; all his angels, praise him; all his hosts praise him; sun and moon praise him; all the shining stars praise him; the heaven of heavens praises the Lord, and the waters above the heavens; they all praise the name of the Lord, for he commanded and they were created, and he established them forever and ever; he made a decree which shall not pass away; praise the Lord from the earth, sea monsters and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and frost, stormy wind fulfilling his word; mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and maidens, old men and children; let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone is exalted." In Psalm 150: "Praise God in his holy place; praise him in his mighty firmament; praise him for his mighty acts; praise him according to his excellent greatness; praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with harp and lyre; every breath praises the Lord."

Since the glorification of all created things is a matter clear to understanding and evident in its importance, and they deserved punishment for not understanding it, through not reflecting upon created things as they should be reflected upon, He alerted them that their well-being is only due to His forbearance toward them; He gives them respite until the term He has set for them, for He does not hasten, in order to affirm His transcendence above every trace of deficiency, to which every thing has testified by declaring Him free of it. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿Indeed He is ever Forbearing﴾; in that He does not hasten to punish you for your turning away from directing your thoughts to what He has commanded you to direct them to.

Since it is generally the case with human beings that when a forbearing person becomes angry he does not forgive, and if he pardons, his pardon is tainted, He (Exalted) said: ﴿Forgiving﴾; indicating by the form of intensity that He is other than that, encouraging repentance.

When He had established, in the context of tawhid, that they are at the very bottom of heedlessness, He turned to the lord of those endowed with understanding, saying (alluding to prophethood, and conjoining with "they do not understand" [in the previous verse], to alert that they do not grasp the tongue of speech, let alone the tongue of circumstance): ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an﴾, which no admonisher can approach and no explainer can equal, and which is an explanation of everything; ﴿We place﴾, meaning, by the greatness We possess; ﴿between you﴾ and them. But He made this implied subject explicit with a descriptive attribute that alerts to their turning away from listening, in the manner that conveys [the meaning]; so He (exalted be He) said: ﴿and between those who do not believe﴾, meaning, for whom faith does not renew itself; ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, meaning, which is the pole of faith; ﴿a barrier﴾, filling everything that is between you and them, while being a veil over you so that they do not perceive you as you truly are; ﴿concealed﴾ from them and from others, seen only by whom We will. That is more emphatic in greatness, and more wondrous in the penetration of the word.

﴿وجَعَلْنا﴾ means: by what We possess of majesty (بِما لَنا مِنَ العَظَمَةِ). ﴿عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ أكِنَّةً﴾ means: coverings (أغْطِيَةً), ﴿أنْ يَفْقَهُوهُ﴾ means: out of aversion, so that they would not understand the Qur'an with its true understanding. ﴿وفِي آذانِهِمْ وقْرًا﴾ means: something heavy (شَيْئًا ثَقِيلًا) that prevents their hearing from being beneficial hearing, due to their deficiency in comprehension (بِالقُصُورِ في إدْراكِهِمْ), not in its clarity (لا في بَيانِهِ). (p-٤٢٩) Therefore their seeing the Prophet ﷺ while he recited is not sound, just as their hearing and comprehension of what he recites is likewise not sound, as He (Exalted) said: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. ﴿وإذا ذَكَرْتَ رَبَّكَ﴾ means: the One who is good to you and to them. ﴿فِي القُرْآنِ﴾ means: while it is ﴿وحْدَهُ﴾, alone, with turning away from their gods. ﴿ولَّوْا﴾ means: they turned away. He confirmed the meaning and depicted it in a way that increases its ugliness, to repel them from it, so He said: ﴿عَلى أدْبارِهِمْ نُفُورًا﴾ ("backward, in flight"). The word نُفُورًا is a verbal noun from a non-matching root, serving as emphasis, because it conveys its meaning; or it is the plural of نافِرٌ, like قاعِدٌ and قُعُودٌ.

The root و-ق-ر, in all its fifteen permutations, revolves around the concept of gathering (الجَمْعِ), as has passed at the end of Surah Yusuf and the beginning of al-Hijr. Thus al-Waqr (with fatha) means: heaviness in the ear, or the complete loss of hearing, because that necessitates a gathering in the self and a stillness that leads to gravity (الوَقارِ), which is tranquility (السَّكِينَةُ), by the loss of some of what would scatter thought from hearing. From this is al-Wiqr (with kasra): a load in general, or a heavy one; or because a load gathers what is in it, and the ear gathers what blocks it, so it is as if it gathered its opening and made it hard like a deaf rock that nothing penetrates. For this reason deafness is called aṣ-ṣamam. Also "nakhlatun muwaqqirah" means a palm laden with a load (مُسْتَجْمِعَةٌ حِمْلًا). "Istawqarat al-ibil" means the camels became fat, i.e., gathered fat and flesh. "Waqara," like "wada'a," means he sat, because some of his limbs gathered toward others. Al-Waqīr means a flock of sheep, or their young, or five hundred of them, or generally, or sheep with their dog, donkey and shepherd, like al-qirah, because some of it gathers toward the rest. Al-Waqariyy (vowelled with fatha and kasra) means the shepherd of the flock, or the owner of sheep, or the owner of donkeys, or the inhabitants of a city. Al-Qirrah, like 'iddah, means dependents, burden, and an elderly great man, because old age and heaviness produce gravity, which arises from gathering the self and resolve, and abandoning scatteredness through frivolity. What precedes them is clear regarding gathering. Al-Muwaqqar, like mu'azzam, means the experienced intelligent one whom the ages have tested, because that produces gathered intellect. "Waqqartu al-rajul tawqiran" means I honoured the man and made him grave; and "al-dabbah" means I calmed the animal, so it is as if a heavy load was gathered onto it. At-Taywqur is faw'ul from gravity (al-waqar), its ta' substituted from a wāw; it is said: "waqara fi baytihi yaqarru," meaning he gathered himself in it, because his concern gathered. Al-Mawqir, like majlis, means the easy place at the foot of a mountain; perhaps it was likened to the grave man, calm, tranquil in self, and the carrier whom the load makes steady. Al-Waqrah means a pit (wakta), i.e., a hollow, found in the hoof, the eye, or the stone, because the nature of a hollow is to gather what is placed in it. From this "tawqir al-shay'" means to make for it waqarat, i.e., marks. Al-Waqr means a crack in the leg; and like the wakta, or the hazmah, found in bone, stone or eye. "Awqara Allahu al-dabbah" means God struck the animal with a waqrah. "Faqir waqir" means broken in bones, or in the spine; or a likening to young sheep; or an imitation; or the meaning that debt weighed him down (awqarahu). Al-Waqir means a great notch in a rock that holds water; and it is clear regarding gathering.

Al-Rawq means a horn, because of the intensity of its gathering, its hardness, its roundness, and because it gathers its owner's boldness and resolve. Al-Rawaq also means a man's resolve and action, because they gather his affair. Ar-Rawaq min al-layl means a portion (of the night), because its hours gather. Rawaq al-bayt means its canopy, i.e., the curtain beneath the upper curtain, because it completes its gathering for the purpose of concealment. Riwaq al-bayt, like kitab and ghurab, means what surrounds it. Al-Qazzaz said: it is said that ar-riwaq is like a tent, held on a single pole in its middle. In al-Qamus he said: or a roof at the front of the house, and the eyebrow of the eye; perhaps it was likened to a covering. Min al-layl means its front and side, likened to the side of the house. Rawq min ash-shabab means its beginning, like ar-rayq, with fatha; and ar-riyq, like kis; its origin is rayawiq, because what follows is built upon it and gathers toward it, as if it were the root that gathers all the branches. Ar-riyq also means that a little rain strikes you; as if it were the first of the rain. Ar-ruqah means a small amount, and it is from this. Ar-rawq also means lifetime, because it gathers the state. Raqanī ash-shay' means it pleased me, because thought gathers the thoughts for its sake, so the face of what made him pleased does not appear. Wasif ruqah means when it pleases you; jariyah ruqah; ghilman ruqah, the plural of raa'iq. Ar-ruqah means a very beautiful thing. Ar-rawq, with fatha, means admiration and wonder at a thing; and of horses, one of good form that pleases the beholder. Al-jamal ar-raa'iq, ar-rayq, ar-rawq, and ar-riwaq mean a curtain, because it gathers sight and concern away from what is behind it. It is also the place of the hunter, because it gathers him toward what he wants and brings him to it. Ar-rawq means the canopy, the front of the house; the brave who cannot be overcome, because his concern gathers toward what he wants; the tent; the lord, for gathering virtues; and clear water and other liquids, because clarity is more fitting for the gathering of parts. Ar-rawq means a group, and pure love, and the verbal noun of "raqa 'alayhi," meaning he increased upon him in excess, because increase only comes from gathering. Ar-rawq means the body of a thing, for it gathers it; and a snake, for its coiling, i.e., its gathering. "Dahiyah dhat rawqayn" means a great calamity likened to a bull (p-٤٣٣). "Rama bi-arwaqihi 'ala ad-dabbah" means he mounted it, i.e., with all his limbs; "rama bi-arwaqihi 'anha" means he dismounted; "alqa arwaqahu" means he ran and his running became intense, as if he came out of all his limbs, so he ran a spirit without a body, and became greater than the bird, i.e., his spirit overcame his body. "Alqa arwaqahu" also means he settled in the place calmly. Al-Qamus said: it seems to be an antonym; end quote. The object of place in this is omitted; as if he said: "in such and such a place." It is known that if his body is in a place while he is alive, then he has settled in it. "Alqa 'alayka arwaqahu" means that you love him intensely; the meaning is that he clothed you with his body, so your spirit directs it, and you become him. Al-Qazzaz's expression, "it is that you love him until you are consumed in his love," indicates this. "Alqat as-sahabah arwaqaha" means its rain and its heavy downpour, or its clear waters; and that is the totality of what is in it. Arwaq al-layl means the midst of its darkness, likened to a tent; "min al-ayn" means its sides, because it contains them. Al-Qazzaz's expression: "daraba al-layl bi-arwaqihi" means when it stood and became fixed. It is said: arwaquhu means its fronts. "Aslabat al-ayn arwaqaha" means its tears flowed, i.e., all that was in it; as if that were a metaphor for the intensity of weeping. Rawq al-faras means the spear that the rider extends from his lance between the ears, likened to the horn of a bull; "dhalika al-faras arwaq," and from it ar-rawaq, with fatha, which is the length of the teeth, likened to the rawq, i.e., the horn; al-Qazzaz said: it is said that ar-rawaq is the length of the teeth, their bending inward into the mouth, and the upper overhanging the lower. "Al-qawm ruq" when they are like that; it is suitable to be a likeness to what was mentioned, and to be from the gathering because of the bending. From it, "akala fulanun rawqahu" means when he grew old, so his life lengthened, until his teeth, likened to horns, fell out. At-tarwiq means purification; it has already passed that when a thing is freed from other things, its parts are more tightly adhering. At-tarwiq means that he sells a commodity and buys a better one from it, likened to purification. Ar-rawuq means a strainer, by which drink is strained without pressing; the cup itself, the bowl, and the wine-pitcher; and the sieve of the drink by which it is strained; because they gather the drink. Al-qaru means intent and pursuit, like extrapolation, induction, and stabbing (p-٤٣٥), and it is clear regarding gathering. Al-qaru means a long basin that camels visit; the expression of al-Qazzaz: a sort of long, extended basin beside the great basin, from which it is emptied into the great basin, visited by camels and sheep; and likewise if it is of wood. Al-qaru means the earth that is hardly cut, as if it protected the gathering of its parts from anyone separating them. Al-qaru means the channel of the press and its trough, because of the gathering of what flows in it; the bottom of the palm, which is hollowed out and drink is stored in it, or a trough and basin made from it for drinking; a cup or small vessel; a dog's drinking place; a lid over a tray; and a pool of water. The Arabs say: "asbahat al-ard qaran wahidan" when fertility and rain abound; and all of that is clear regarding gathering. It also means the swelling of the two testicles from wind or water, or the descent of the intestines, like al-qarwah; this is either because of their resemblance to the cup, or because of their gathering what caused their enlargement. Qura, like fu'la, means water in the desert, because it gathers people. Al-qura means a gourd that is eaten, because it is suitable to be made into a vessel. Al-qara means the back, because it gathers the limbs. Naqah qarwa'u means a she-camel with a long hump. Al-maqruri means one with a long back. Aqra means he complained; either it is from the complaint of the back, or it is for negation, i.e., he removed the gathering of his concern and resolve. Al-qarwa' (p-٤٣٦) means custom, because it gathers its people; and the rear, because it gathers what is in it. Aqra means he sought hospitality and was bound to hospitality. Aqra al-jull 'ala al-faras means he bound it upon him. Al-maqariyy means the heads of hills, because they gather. Taraktuhum qaran wahidan means in a single manner, i.e., gathered together. Shatun maqrawwah means its head was placed in a piece of wood so that it would not suckle itself, i.e., its two jaws were gathered. Qarwat ar-ra's means its extremity; the expression of al-Qazzaz: and qarwan ar-ra's; qarwat ar-ra's means its top, as if it were the gathering place of his affair, because it is the place of thought. Qarwat al-anf means its tip, because it is the last gatherer of its beauty. Istaqra ad-dummal means pus settled in it, i.e., gathered. Al-qayrawan means the bulk of an army and the bulk of a caravan. The remainder of the root will come, God willing (Exalted), in: ﴿بِوَرِقِكم هَذِهِ﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], in "al-Kahf."

When they (the disbelievers) at times claimed to hear and understand, and thereby cast doubt upon some whose faith was not firmly rooted, He (Exalted is He) followed this with what confirms what has passed and strengthens the listeners in it. So He (Exalted is He) said, in the manner of a reply, threatening and indicating that their faculties are known: ﴿We know best﴾, i.e., more than any knower, ﴿what they listen to﴾, i.e., how intently they give ear and incline, seeking to hear ﴿with it﴾, from their ears and hearts; or, ﴿because of it﴾, from their desire to catch a slip which they make a point of denying and mocking. ﴿When﴾, i.e., at the time when, ﴿they listen﴾, i.e., they give ear with all their effort. He made clear their spiritual distance by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿when they are a secret conference, when﴾, i.e., and at the time when, ﴿they are﴾ engaged in ﴿secret conference﴾, i.e., they confer privately, each one of them conveying his secret to his companion, after turning away from listening. Then He mentioned the time of the secret conference, saying (Exalted is He): ﴿when the wrongdoers say﴾, disclosing their inner state by a description indicating what drove them to what they conferred about; and they are the ﴿wrongdoers﴾. Their saying was: ﴿You follow only a man bewitched﴾, i.e., one whose mind is deranged. By this description they reached the summit of wrongdoing. The secret of using the passive participle in place of the active participle will come at the end of the surah.

Then he linked to that proof their attribution, glorified is He, to ignorance, which was the consequence of their saying this. So He (exalted) said: ﴿Look﴾. And since their situation is one that greatly increases wonder, and the motives to ask about it are abundant, He (exalted) said: ﴿how they have struck for you the examples﴾; that is, these misguided ones, ﴿for you the examples﴾, which are the furthest thing from your attributes, from their saying: "a sorcerer," "a poet," "a madman," and the like. ﴿So they have strayed﴾ from the truth in all of that; ﴿so they cannot﴾, that is, as a result of their straying it follows that they ﴿cannot find a way﴾, that is, a path they could take, toward striking upon a parable or firmly establishing a matter in an action. This comes after Allah forbade them with His saying (exalted): ﴿So do not strike for Allah examples. Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know﴾ [an-Nahl: 74]. So this is, as it were, the first proof of what we described them with, of lacking understanding and hearing, let alone that they should have any path to opposing this Qur'an, which they claim is the speech of a human, or that they could cast doubt upon it with some dubious argument, let alone with a proof.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 49:

When the custom of the Qur'an was to establish tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, and the return (al-ma'ad); and it presented the proofs for the first two; and it concluded by affirming their ignorance regarding prophethood despite its clear evidence; it followed this with a clear matter concerning their straying from the path regarding the question of the return; and it established it to the utmost degree of establishment, and clarified it in the most complete clarification. So He (Exalted is He) said, marveling at them: ﴿And they say﴾; that is, the polytheists, who deny tawhid, prophethood, and resurrection, despite their acknowledgment that We began their creation, and their witnessing at every moment that We bring the earth back to life after its death: ﴿"When﴾; as a rhetorical interrogation of denial, as if they were certain of the non-occurrence of what they deny. The governing element of "idha" (when) is a verb derived from the word "mab'uthun" (resurrected), not the word itself, since what follows "inna" does not govern what precedes it. The meaning is: Will we be resurrected when ﴿we have become﴾; that is, with the totality of our bodies, as a settled state; ﴿bones and crumbled dust﴾; that is, broken, pulverized debris; and dust; ﴿"Will we indeed be resurrected﴾ while being ﴿created anew"?﴾

So it was as if it were said: "Then what will be said to them in reply?" It was said: "Say" (﴿قُلْ﴾) to them: "Do not be dust-fragments (rufat); rather, ﴿be﴾ (﴿كُونُوا﴾) dust; rather, be the hardest of dust, ﴿stones﴾ (﴿حِجارَةً﴾), that is, in the utmost degree of dryness; ﴿or iron﴾ (﴿أوْ حَدِيدًا﴾), which adds to the dryness of stones the intensity of the cohesion of its parts."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 51:
