And the land from which he had wanted to drive them out, which is the land of Egypt, is meant. That is: become such that you dwell in it, with no hand over you and no one to prevent you from what you wish from it, as Pharaoh and his soldiers were, whenever you wish, given possession of it, after you had been slaves subjected to the worst torment. ﴿So when there comes﴾, that is, a certain coming, ﴿the promise of the Hereafter﴾, that is, the Resurrection, after you have dwelt in the land alive and been buried in it dead, ﴿We will bring you﴾, that is, by the majesty We possess, ﴿all together﴾ from it, that is, We will raise you and them mixed together, with no ruling of one over another and no defense of one against another, in a state other than that which was in the world. Then We will separate (p. 530) some of you from others, and We will grant the good among you comfort by humiliating the wicked.

If the Children of Israel, whose words these polytheistic ignoramuses accept and whose counsel they seek in their affairs, are asked about this which We have recited to you, they will report it as We have told you, and the matter of the Hereafter will then be established for them. Otherwise, their acceptance of some of their scripture and rejection of other parts would be without any proof, arbitrary, and a preference without any preferring cause.

When the reality of the Gathering (hashr) was established, through demonstrating power over every possible thing at one point, and through informing the Children of Israel, who had bound themselves to accept what he said and had traveled the deserts to him to ask about some other matters, it was established that this Qur'an, which reports that, is true. They had asked him about the matters mentioned, and he answered them about the first of them, which is the Spirit (al-Ruh), with a general answer. He followed this by noting that they had asked him about things they had proposed, saying, "We will not believe you until you do them." By reporting the signs of Moses (peace be upon him), He (Exalted) indicated that He did not withhold answering them out of stinginess or incapacity, since those signs were of the same kind as what they asked for: the control of waters, at one time by sending them down and at another by turning them into blood, which necessitates the power to make trees grow by them, and the causing of the heaven to fall in pieces, by the sending down of destructive hail. Thus the soundness of the report of the varied examples (tasrif al-amthal) in this Book was established. (p-531) So He joined to His saying, "And We have varied": His saying (Exalted), ﴿And with the truth﴾, meaning: from the established meanings about which there is no doubt, not by anything else. ﴿We sent it down﴾, We, the Qur'an, or this which reported of the gathering to the Children of Israel, who were surrounded by the Copts, and what came before it, according to the greatness that is Ours. ﴿And with the truth﴾, not by anything else, ﴿it descended﴾, and it reached them through your tongue after its being sent down to you, just as We sent it down, identically, fresh and new, preserved, with nothing having befallen it, so there is nothing in it of distortion or alteration, as occurred in the book of the Jews, whom your people ask. This indicates that the Qur'an is miraculous by its being, together with its inimitability, eloquent in the varying of examples and in other arrangements of discourse. ﴿And We did not send you﴾, meaning: with what We have of greatness, ﴿except as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾, with complete firmness in each of the two descriptions, as indicated by the conjunction (wa) and the form of the word. You convey to them what it contains of good news for whoever believes in that Day, and of warning for whoever does not believe in it. If they accept, it is their share; and if they do not accept, its burden falls upon them, and there is no blame upon you, for We did not send you as a guardian over them. We will surely crush their falsehood by this truth, without doubt, so do not hasten on their behalf. "Indeed, falsehood was ever bound to vanish." We did not send you to make rivers gush forth, nor to make trees grow.

Then He informed that the wisdom in sending down the Qur'an in installments (munajjaman) is that He said (Exalted is He): ﴿And a Qur'an﴾; meaning: and We have distinguished (faṣṣalnā); or: and We sent down; a Qur'an; ﴿which We have divided﴾; meaning: We sent it down in installments (munajjaman) over lengthy periods of time (p-532); and We distinguished it by truth from every falsehood, and by its inimitability from every speech; ﴿that you may recite it to the people at intervals﴾; meaning: to the common people, all of those among them whom you are able to reach; for you are sent to all of them.

And since they, because of their restlessness (naws), were in the utmost agitation, not becoming refined except over long periods of time and great treatment, He said, pointing to that: ﴿at a measured pace﴾; meaning: with deliberation and deliberate recitation, by reciting from it each installment at the time in which We sent it down, over a period of twenty-three years; ﴿And We have sent it down﴾; from Us, by virtue of the greatness We possess; ﴿in gradual revelation﴾; some of it following upon some other, divided according to the events, because that is more precise in explaining them and more helpful for understanding, owing to the long reflection on what was revealed of its installments during the interval between two installments, because of the abundance of meanings in it and the multitude of wisdoms it contains; and that is also closer to memorization and greater in making the heart firm and more expansive for the breast, because when the news of the Beloved is continuous, the lover is every day in a festival, with a fresh delight. We have done that with you for what has preceded, namely that Allah is with those who are God-fearing and those who are doers of good.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 107:

When the proofs had grown long, the doubts had been removed, and it was known that good fortune belongs to whoever turns toward it and misfortune to whoever turns away, He commanded His Messenger to say, alerting them to this and rebuking them for their holding back from it and their obstinacy regarding it, through His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Say: Believe in it﴾; that is, the Qur'an, ﴿or do not believe﴾. Belief in it does not need you, nor does it depend upon you, for if you believe in it, the good fortune is yours, and if not, you harm only yourselves. This is a belittling of them, since He has varied for them every kind of example, yet they refused everything except disbelief. Then He gave a reason for this that appeals to every person of understanding. If "Say" is addressed to him, then it is a consolation for him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace; and if it is for what follows it, then it is a rebuke to them and a belittling. So He said (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed those who were given knowledge﴾. He used the passive form to indicate that divine knowledge, which is knowledge in reality from whatever source it comes, urges belief in this Qur'an, and as an alert that whoever possesses knowledge yet whose knowledge does not lead him to believe in this Book, about whose truth nothing is clearer, by its confirming the books of the prophets whose messages were established, whose ages have passed over them, and in which souls have found rest, and by its surpassing them through what Allah has deposited in it of inimitability and wisdom, then his knowledge is as if it were no knowledge; indeed he is the most ignorant of the ignorant, whether he is one of those you asked about me or one of others, as will come, Allah willing (exalted is He), its verification in "The Groups" (az-Zumar).

Since the intended meaning is that whoever is characterized by this attribute, even for a brief time, benefits from it, He introduced the preposition, saying, encouraging toward knowledge so as to lead to belief in the Qur'an: ﴿from before it﴾; that is, before its revelation, from among those of the Children of Israel who believed, whom Allah commanded me to ask, as a means of making you hear and as a confirmation that you turned to them with questions and made them the object of trust; ﴿when it is recited﴾; that is, by whatever reciter it is, ﴿upon them﴾, at any time, moving them from state to state, elevating them along the stages of nearness and the ascents of perfection to the highest ranks, so that they ﴿fall down﴾; that is, they drop swiftly. He emphasized the swiftness and indicated exclusivity by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿upon their chins﴾, with the preposition lam rather than "ila" or "ala," indicating by "the chins" that from the intensity of the humility that comes over them they fall in the manner of one who has no choice. The first part of the body to meet the ground in the fall of such a person is his chin, which is the junction of the two jaws from the place where the beard grows. A human being is naturally inclined to protect his face, so he raises his head, and his chin and mouth become the nearest part of his face to the ground at the moment of falling. For this reason their poet said:

"...... ∗∗∗ so he fell prostrate upon the two hands and the mouth."

Then He made clear that this is not a fall compelled from every direction, through His saying (exalted is He): ﴿prostrating﴾; that is, they do this because of what they know of its truth through the earlier knowledge they were given, and the submission and fear of the Most Merciful that is in their hearts;

﴿And they say﴾, meaning in a continuous, repeated manner; ﴿Glory be to our Lord﴾, meaning exalted is the One who brought us into being, who manages our affairs, and who is good to us, above any defect of imperfection, because He promised through the tongues of His messengers that He would resurrect us after death. His promise is true, so it must come to pass. He also promised that this Book would come through the tongue of this Arab Prophet, and He conveyed this promise to us in the earlier scriptures. So He fulfilled what His promise had already announced. ﴿Indeed﴾, meaning, He ﴿was﴾, meaning in an unbreakable state of being, ﴿the promise of our Lord﴾, meaning of the One who is good to us by granting faith and what follows from it of the forms of knowledge, ﴿is surely fulfilled﴾ without failure. All that He promised of reward and punishment will certainly come to pass. This is an allusion to the Quraysh, who used to mock the threat in their saying: "Or you make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed" (﴿Or you make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾), and the like, whose meaning is an attack on the power of God, who is capable of all things.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 17, verse 109:

﴿And they fall upon their faces﴾; at the recitation of it; ﴿weeping﴾, along with their prostration; ﴿and it increases them in﴾ ﴿humility﴾ — its repetition; ﴿khushu'an﴾, that is: submission, humbleness, and lowliness; so if your question to them was so that you would believe when they inform you that I am upon the truth, then believe; but if it was for other than that, then your foolishness, the weakness of your affair, and the badness of your opinion have become clear. He expressed the weeping with the verb, as an indication of its renewal at certain times, because they have, at some times, joy over some of the pleasures that were permitted; and with the noun for prostration, as an indication of the continuance of their humbling themselves through the prescribed prostration, or through humility in general. What will increase this clarity will come in surah Maryam.

[p. 536] Since the first people of knowledge believed in it, submitted to it, and abandoned their religions, which they had taken from the prophets who came to them with the Scriptures for this purpose, after the decisive proof was established that it is from Allah, it becomes obligatory for everyone who has even the slightest humanity to believe in it, turn to it, and call upon the One who sent it down, alone and not others, always, not only in times of hardship. ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish except Him.﴾ The times of answered supplication are more fitting for prayer than others, and the state of prostration, especially with weeping and humility, is the best of them, as in the saying: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." The obstinate Arabs were, as it were, saying (because that is their character and their right after the proofs had been established): "We believe, so teach us how to call upon Him and by which name to cry out." Since "Allah" is the name that comprises all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names, and since it is mentioned in Surah an-Nahl with an emphasis not found in other surahs, for the secrets already mentioned, and although it counts among the blessings mentioned there the teaching of man to speak clearly, which is most fitting to the name "the Most Merciful" (﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾, the verses), and since mercy, worldly and otherworldly, from the Creator and from creatures, has been repeated in this surah eight times: ﴿Perhaps your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾; ﴿the wing of humility out of mercy﴾; [p. 537] ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them both﴾; ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾; ﴿Your Lord knows best about you; if He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾; ﴿Indeed He has ever been Merciful to you﴾; ﴿except as a mercy from your Lord﴾; ﴿the treasures of my Lord's mercy﴾; and since this was evident in the intention of its generality, the name "the Most Merciful" was most fitting for it. The answer came in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful﴾; that is: the Supreme King, Possessor of majesty and honour, in the essence of His all-encompassing reality, ﴿or call upon the Most Merciful﴾, in the sense of His being absolutely pervaded by mercy. That is: name Him, that is, direct your supplication while naming Him in the state of your calling, your Lord whom you glorified in prostration, by whatever name you wish from among those He has permitted. So cry out with this name that indicates majesty and the deserving of its named reality of supplication for its own essence, or with this name that indicates beauty and the deserving of supplication for His general bounty, and in the state of prostration. ﴿Whichever you call﴾, that is, by any of His names, you have attained the aim, for the Named is one, even though His names indicating nobility are many. Since "the Most Merciful" contains an apparent beauty with an inner majesty, because the generality of mercy includes some bounty and some gradual leading on and punishment, it was therefore comprehensive of all the Most Beautiful Names and the Lofty Attributes. He attached to the mention of each of the two names the comprehensive knowledge and the descriptive term in its proper place, saying: ﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾; that is, to the One named by these two names alone, who is the One, the Unique, ﴿the Most Beautiful Names﴾, these two names [p. 538] and others, from what has come from the Prophet (ﷺ), which indicate praise, glorification, sanctification and exaltation. This pronoun is an instance of *istikhdam* (a usage in which a pronoun returns to a different sense than its antecedent). This saying implies that the meaning of the name "the Most Merciful" is more comprehensive than "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), although the form of each of them is for intensification.

Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali (may Allah have mercy on him), in his explanation of the Most Beautiful Names, said: "*Al-Rahmaniyyah* is the absorption of creation in mercy at their origination, and *al-Rahimiyyah* is the directing of creation toward what agrees with their senses, suits their creation, their character, and the aim of their hearts. When this is specific to some, it is *rahimiyyah*; when it is absolute, it is *rahmaniyyah*. Because the meaning of the name "the Most Merciful" is absolute, the perfection of its meaning was not present in creation, so it did not truly apply to any of them; rather, a particular portion of its meaning is found in them, by which the name "the Most Merciful" applies to them, not the name "the Most Merciful" in the absolute sense. Therefore, the name "the Most Merciful" is attached, in the sense of its absoluteness, to the name Allah in the reality of its all-encompassing essence. So He said (exalted is He): ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾. When the heart truly recognizes His exclusivity to Allah by knowledge, it becomes the root for uttering it with the tongue. You know that there is no *Rahman* except Allah, just as there is no *Ilah* except Allah, and it is attached to the name *al-Ilah*. The lack of the perfection of its meaning in creation is known, just as the root of the knowledge of consideration is missing from its meaning in the name *Ilah*. Monotheism in the name *al-Rahman* is obligatory, attached to the obligation in the monotheism of *al-Ilah*. For this reason the name Allah was placed first in its occurrences in the Books, and in this enumeration, that is, in what occurs in [p. 539] the hadith of al-Tirmidhi, al-Bazzar and others, of the Most Beautiful Names of Allah, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)." End of quotation.

It has already passed at the end of Surah al-Hijr what is beneficial here.

Since He mentioned prostration and followed it with supplication, He indicated that it is good in every state, and better and more excellent in prayer, after having recently mentioned the five prayers. It may have been understood from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation at dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra' 78] and His saying: ﴿when it is recited to them﴾ [al-Isra' 107], that there is strength in reciting it aloud. He said (exalted is He): ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud﴾; that is, your recitation in it; or He called the recitation "prayer" because it is a condition of it; aloud with strength, so that the polytheists might hear it. For the opponents' obstinacy is well known, so there is no assurance that they will not revile the Qur'an, him who sent it down, and him who brought it. Rather, they used to do this and make noise, and sometimes they clapped and whistled in order to confuse the Prophet (ﷺ) and mix up his recitation. ﴿Nor be silent in it﴾; that is, do not whisper; ﴿in it﴾, whispering with great quietness, as if you were discussing it with another, such that you do not make those behind you hear, so that they may take it from you. ﴿And seek﴾; that is, strive with all your effort, ﴿between that﴾; that is, between loudness and quietness, which the distance particle indicates to be of great importance, ﴿a way﴾; that is, a middle path.

Al-Bukhari, in the Book of *Tafsir*, related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) concerning this verse that he said: "It was revealed while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was hiding in Mecca. When he led his companions in prayer, he raised his voice with the Qur'an. [p. 540] When the polytheists heard it, they reviled the Qur'an, him who sent it down, and him who brought it. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud﴾, that is, your recitation, so that the polytheists hear it and revile the Qur'an; ﴿nor be silent in it﴾, from your companions, so that you do not make them hear." End of quotation.

Here he applied the name of the whole to the part, indicating that the intended meaning is the prayer. Earlier, the name of the part was applied to the whole, because the greater intention there was the recitation at dawn. Al-Bukhari related from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that this verse was revealed concerning supplication. It has been mentioned more than once that it is no strange thing for a matter to have many causes.

(p-541) When the all-encompassing nature of these two names had preceded, namely that "Allah" encompasses all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names, and that "al-Rahman" encompasses the quality of mercy, the one commanded to call upon them both, every addressee, (ﷺ) was singled out by the command to praise, the meaning of which is all-encompassing, and his name (ﷺ) is derived from it, because he possesses it, being both one who praises (ḥāmid) and one who is praised (maḥmūd). He was also commanded to magnify (Allah) above anything the servants may understand of His Most Beautiful Names. So (He, Exalted) said: ﴿Say: Praise belongs to Allah﴾, that is, the comprehensive ascription of the most beautiful attributes, ﴿to Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿who has not taken a son﴾, because He encompasses the most beautiful attributes, ﴿for having a son is not done except out of need, and need is among the worst of attributes﴾. ﴿Nor has He had any partner in dominion﴾, that is, He does not exist in any way whatsoever, ﴿neither a son nor other than him, for that does not occur except through weakness﴾. ﴿Nor has He had any protector﴾, a helper, more general than whether that helper is a son, a partner, or other than these. Then he qualified it by describing it, saying (Exalted): ﴿out of humiliation﴾, to convey that He has protégés whom He favored with nearness and made helpers of His religion, out of His mercy toward them, not out of any need on His part for them. ﴿And magnify Him﴾, exalting Him above having anyone share with Him in anything, and above anything that a understanding person may comprehend or any describer may describe. Magnification (al-takbīr) is the most eloquent expression in Arabic for the meaning of glorification and reverence; this was said by Abu Hayyan. He emphasized it with the verbal noun to confirm and intensify its meaning, that is, He said: ﴿with magnification﴾, exalting Him beyond anyone attaining the full reality of His knowledge, or anyone being ignorant of Him in every respect. Rather, He, glorified is He, veiled Himself by His majesty and grandeur, so He is not known, and He manifested Himself by His generosity and perfection, so He is not denied. Thus the explicit meaning of ascribing praise to Him is that He, Exalted, possesses all attributes of perfection, and the explicit meaning of describing Him by negating what was mentioned is that He is free (tanzīh, declaring Allah exempt from every imperfection) from any trace of deficiency, and that He is greater than anything that occurs to servants who are created with deficiency and disposed to the instincts of weakness. For this reason, and for other great meanings, the Prophet (ﷺ) named this verse the Verse of Might, as related by Imam Ahmad from Sahl, from his father, may Allah be pleased with them both. This is the very substance with which the surah opened, of declaring Allah free of imperfection, with an addition. And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final resort.
